items.content: The European AI Office supports the development and adoption of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions, while protecting people against risks. The European AI Office was established within the European Commission as the foundation for a single AI governance system. It supports the EU approach to AI , playing a key role in implementing the AI Act – especially for general-purpose AI (GPAI) – guaranteeing the health, safety and fundamental rights of people and providing legal certainty to businesses. It also enforces the rules for GPAI models and supports the governance bodies in Member States in their tasks. This is underpinned by the powers given to the Commission by the AI Act, including the ability to conduct evaluations of GPAI models, request information and measures from model providers, and apply sanctions. The AI Office also promotes an innovative ecosystem of trustworthy AI , to reap the societal and economic benefits. It ensures a strategic, coherent and effective European approach to AI at international level , becoming a global reference point. The Structure of the AI Office The AI Office employs more than 125 staff, including technology specialists, administrative assistants, lawyers, policy specialists, and economists. It has 6 units and 2 advisers, reflecting its mandate: “Excellence in AI and Robotics” - unit A1 “Regulation and Compliance” - unit A2 “AI Safety” - unit A3 “AI Innovation and Policy Coordination” - unit A4 “AI for Societal Good” - unit A5 "AI in Health and Life Science" - unit A6 Lead Scientific Adviser International Affairs Adviser Tasks of the AI Office Supporting the AI Act and enforcing general-purpose AI rules The AI Office makes use of its expertise to support the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act by: Contributing to the coherent application of the AI Act across the Member States, including the set-up of advisory bodies at EU level, facilitating support and information exchange Developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks for evaluating capabilities and reach of general-purpose AI models, and classifying models with systemic risks Drawing up state-of-the-art codes of practice to detail out rules, in cooperation with leading AI developers, the scientific community and other experts Preparing guidance and guidelines, implementing and delegated acts , and other tools to support effective implementation of the AI Act and monitor compliance with the regulation Investigating possible infringements of the rules, including inspections, requests for technical documentation and access to models in order to assess models' capabilities Requesting providers to take corrective action and, in case of infringement, restrict the public availability of a model and issue direct fines for non-compliance Strengthening the development and use of trustworthy AI The AI Office, in collaboration with relevant public and private actors and the startup community, contributes to fostering trustworthy AI across the EU by: Advancing actions and policies to reap the societal and economic benefits of AI across the EU Providing advice on best practices and enabling ready-access to AI sandboxes, real-world testing and other European support structures for AI uptake Encouraging innovative ecosystems of trustworthy AI to enhance the EU’s competitiveness and economic growth Aiding the Commission in leveraging the use of transformative AI tools and reinforcing AI literacy Fostering international cooperation At international level, the AI Office contributes to a strategic, coherent, and effective EU approach, by: Promoting the EU’s approach to trustworthy AI , including collaboration with similar institutions worldwide Fostering international cooperation and governance on AI, contributing to a global approach to AI Supporting the development and implementation of international agreements on AI Cooperation with institutions, experts and stakeholders The AI Office collaborates with Member States and the wider expert community through dedicated platforms: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (AI Board) is a key advisory body supported by the AI Office that includes representatives from each EU Member States and the European Centre for Algorithmic Transparency (ECAT). The AI Board’s primary role is to ensure the effective implementation of the AI Act across the EU by coordinating national authorities, sharing technical and regulatory expertise and providing advice on AI policy, innovation, and international partnerships. The Scientific Panel of independent experts ensures a strong link with the scientific community. Further technical expertise is gathered in an Advisory Forum , representing a balanced selection of stakeholders, including industry, startups and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs), academia, think tanks and civil society. The AI Office also oversees the AI Pact , which allows businesses to engage with the Commission and other stakeholders to share best practices and join activities. This engagement has started before the AI Act entered into force and allows businesses to plan ahead and prepare for the full implementation of the AI Act. To stay up to date and register, check the AI Pact events . The Apply AI Alliance is the main coordination forum bringing together AI providers, industry leaders, academia and the public sector to ensure policy actions are grounded in the real-world needs. Closely connected to the Alliance, an AI Observatory will track AI trends and assess impact of AI in specific sectors. Initiatives promoting the development and adoption of AI The AI Office actively supports innovators through policies and initiatives that spur growth across the EU: The AI Continent action plan , launched in April 2025, explains how to harness the untapped potential of EU researchers and industries, turning EU strengths – such as unparalleled talent and strong traditional industries – into AI accelerators. items.raw_text: The European AI Office supports the development and adoption of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions, while protecting people against risks. The European AI Office was established within the European Commission as the foundation for a single AI governance system. It supports the EU approach to AI , playing a key role in implementing the AI Act – especially for general-purpose AI (GPAI) – guaranteeing the health, safety and fundamental rights of people and providing legal certainty to businesses. It also enforces the rules for GPAI models and supports the governance bodies in Member States in their tasks. This is underpinned by the powers given to the Commission by the AI Act, including the ability to conduct evaluations of GPAI models, request information and measures from model providers, and apply sanctions. The AI Office also promotes an innovative ecosystem of trustworthy AI , to reap the societal and economic benefits. It ensures a strategic, coherent and effective European approach to AI at international level , becoming a global reference point. The Structure of the AI Office The AI Office employs more than 125 staff, including technology specialists, administrative assistants, lawyers, policy specialists, and economists. It has 6 units and 2 advisers, reflecting its mandate: “Excellence in AI and Robotics” - unit A1 “Regulation and Compliance” - unit A2 “AI Safety” - unit A3 “AI Innovation and Policy Coordination” - unit A4 “AI for Societal Good” - unit A5 "AI in Health and Life Science" - unit A6 Lead Scientific Adviser International Affairs Adviser Tasks of the AI Office Supporting the AI Act and enforcing general-purpose AI rules The AI Office makes use of its expertise to support the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act by: Contributing to the coherent application of the AI Act across the Member States, including the set-up of advisory bodies at EU level, facilitating support and information exchange Developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks for evaluating capabilities and reach of general-purpose AI models, and classifying models with systemic risks Drawing up state-of-the-art codes of practice to detail out rules, in cooperation with leading AI developers, the scientific community and other experts Preparing guidance and guidelines, implementing and delegated acts , and other tools to support effective implementation of the AI Act and monitor compliance with the regulation Investigating possible infringements of the rules, including inspections, requests for technical documentation and access to models in order to assess models' capabilities Requesting providers to take corrective action and, in case of infringement, restrict the public availability of a model and issue direct fines for non-compliance Strengthening the development and use of trustworthy AI The AI Office, in collaboration with relevant public and private actors and the startup community, contributes to fostering trustworthy AI across the EU by: Advancing actions and policies to reap the societal and economic benefits of AI across the EU Providing advice on best practices and enabling ready-access to AI sandboxes, real-world testing and other European support structures for AI uptake Encouraging innovative ecosystems of trustworthy AI to enhance the EU’s competitiveness and economic growth Aiding the Commission in leveraging the use of transformative AI tools and reinforcing AI literacy Fostering international cooperation At international level, the AI Office contributes to a strategic, coherent, and effective EU approach, by: Promoting the EU’s The AI Office also oversees the AI Pact , which allows businesses to engage with the Commission and other stakeholders to share best practices and join activities. This engagement has started before the AI Act entered into force and allows businesses to plan ahead and prepare for the full implementation of the AI Act. To stay up to date and register, check the AI Pact events . items.content: Nearly 1,000 high-level policymakers, start-ups, industry leaders and researchers will take part in the Apply AI Summit in Brussels tomorrow. They will discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) can boost Europe’s competitiveness across 10 strategic sectors and the public sector. The summit will also showcase concrete AI applications, European success stories and innovative projects. Henna Virkkunen , Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, will host the summit and present the first Apply AI Startup Award to three European start-ups. The award recognises innovative European startups and scaleups developing AI solutions in the strategic sectors. Alongside the in-person event, an online conference platform will run from 16 to 20 November, allowing additional 2,500 participants to join part of the summit. The Apply AI Summit marks one year since the adoption of the Apply AI Strategy , which sets out how to speed up the use of AI in Europe’s key industries and the public sector. It concludes the first European AI Innovation Month , running from 14 October to 17 November 2026, organised by the European Commission in partnership with the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.24896 (cs) [Submitted on 18 Nov 2026] Title: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators Authors: Michael Liaofan Liu , Joe Kileel View a PDF of the paper titled Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators, by Michael Liaofan Liu and Joe Kileel View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures. items.content: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators Michael Liaofan Liu † † thanks: Email: michael.liu.2024@utexas.edu Affiliation: Oden Institute, University of Texas at Austin Joe Kileel Affiliation: Oden Institute, University of Texas at Austin Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Texas at Austin Abstract We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite-dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures. 1 Introduction Many physical systems obey natural symmetries which learned models should respect. For example, changing coordinates in a system of charged particles should affect predicted accelerations according to the change of coordinates, while leaving predicted energies unchanged. Such transformation laws appear throughout science and engineering, and should constrain the class of admissible models. Equivariance formalizes this requirement. Let G G be a group acting on an input space X X and an output space Y Y . In data-driven applications we seek to learn a function F : X → Y F:X\to Y that is G G -equivariant , meaning that F ⁡ ( g ⋅ x ) = g ⋅ F ⁡ ( x ) F(g\cdot x)=g\cdot F(x) for all g ∈ G g\in G and x ∈ X x\in X , i.e., transforming the input and then predicting gives the same result as predicting and then transforming the output. When the action on Y Y leaves every output unchanged, this condition reduces to G G -invariance . A wide variety of approaches exist to encourage or enforce equivariance in machine learning models. For instance, data augmentation [ 48 , 10 ] encourages equivariance by training the model on many transformed copies of input-output pairs, but it does not guarantee equivariance in general. Equivariant multilayer perceptrons [ 20 ] enforce equivariance by solving linear constraints derived from group generators to parameterize equivariant linear layers. Equivariant graph networks [ 53 , 43 ] enforce equivariance through message passing. We investigate an alternative approach that enforces equivariance through polynomial features [ 36 , 59 , 56 ] . The underlying model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomials, called covariants , where the scalar coefficients are arbitrary learned functions of invariant polynomials, called invariants . To formalize this approach, suppose that X X and Y Y are finite-dimensional semisimple real G G -representations [ 21 ] . Suppose first that the target function F F is a polynomial. Then F F lies in the covariant module ℳ ⁡ ( X , Y ) ≔ { G -equivariant polynomial maps from ​ X ​ to ​ Y } . \mathcal{M}(X,Y)\coloneq\{\text{$G$-equivariant polynomial maps from }X\text{ to }Y\}. This is a module over the invariant algebra ℛ ⁡ ( X ) ≔ { G -invariant polynomials from ​ X ​ to ​ ℝ } , \mathcal{R}(X)\coloneq\{\text{$G$-invariant polynomials from }X\text{ to }\mathbb{R}\}, which is an algebra over ℝ \mathbb{R} . By Hilbert’s finiteness theorem (see Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 ), there exist finite generating sets { r 1 , … , r R } \{r_{1},\dots,r_{R}\} for ℛ ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{R}(X) as an ℝ \mathbb{R} -algebra and { m 1 , … , m M } \{m_{1},\dots,m_{M}\} for ℳ ⁡ ( X , Y ) \mathcal{M}(X,Y) as an ℛ ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{R}(X) -module. Thus, there exists a polynomial map p : ℝ R → ℝ M p\colon\mathbb{R}^{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} such that F ⁡ ( x ) = ∑ i = 1 M p i ​ ( r 1 ​ ( x ) , … , r R ​ ( x ) ) ​ m i ​ ( x ) . F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{M}p_{i}(r_{1}(x),\dots,r_{R}(x))m_{i}(x). (1) For arbitrary targets F F , we propose to replace the polynomial p p with a learnable function 𝒩 θ : ℝ R → ℝ M \mathcal{N}_{\theta}\colon\mathbb{R}^{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} , such as a neural network, a random forest, or a kernel regression model. This yields a class of G G -equivariant functions F θ ​ ( x ) = ∑ i = 1 M 𝒩 θ , i ​ ( r 1 ​ ( x ) , … , r R ​ ( x ) ) ​ m i ​ ( x ) , F_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathcal{N}_{\theta,i}(r_{1}(x),\dots,r_{R}(x))m_{i}(x), (2) where the goal is to learn θ \theta so that F θ ≈ F F_{\theta}\approx F . The ansatz can serve as an end-to-end predictor or as an equivariant component within a larger architecture. This model class has appeared before in various forms often under the name of “scalarization” [ 59 , 56 , 6 , 61 , 32 ] , but to our knowledge it has not yet been developed at our level of generality and packaged into a user-friendly toolkit. The work [ 32 ] precedes this one and is most similar. After introducing Eq. ( 2 ), it focused on the case of tensor-valued inputs/outputs, and developed algorithms using binary forms for important applications to fluid dynamics. We observe that the models F θ F_{\theta} are automatically equivariant, because the maps m i m_{i} are equivariant and polynomials r j r_{j} are invariant. Consequently, the learnable coefficient functions 𝒩 θ \mathcal{N}_{\theta} need not satisfy any additional equivariance constraints and can be chosen at will. Thus, the number of parameters in 𝒩 θ \mathcal{N}_{\theta} can be much smaller than in other equivariant networks. As an example, when G = O ⁡ ( d ) G=\operatorname{O}(d) , X = n ​ ℝ d X=n\mathbb{R}^{d} , and Y = ℝ d Y=\mathbb{R}^{d} , the invariant algebra is generated by the pairwise inner products x i ⋅ x j x_{i}\cdot x_{j} , and the covariant module is generated by the coordinate projections ( x 1 , … , x n ) ↦ x j (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\mapsto x_{j} [ 56 , Lemma 1 and Proposition 4] . When G = SO ⁡ ( 3 ) G=\operatorname{SO}(3) , Gordan’s algorithm or more modern variants can be used to compute the generators up to a given degree [ 38 , 32 ] . The e3nn [ 22 ] and lie-nn [ 3 ] packages can be used to compute explicit vector space bases for the homogeneous components of the covariant module and invariant algebra for various groups. One can then apply the graded Nakayama lemma to extract minimal homogeneous generators from these bases. One of our technical contributions is an alternative construction of vector space bases (Theorem 3.4 ) that uses the Cauchy decomposition to factor spaces tracking the action of G G from spaces tracking identical copies of irreducible representations in the input representation. This results in an algorithm (Algorithm 3.9 ) to compute minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and covariant module up to prescribed degrees. We also introduce data structures based on tensor networks to enable efficient storage and evaluation of the invariant and covariant features (Definition 3.5 ). Our method achieves large speedups (Figures 6 and 7 ) compared to a Gordan’s algorithm baseline for SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \operatorname{SO}(3) . Conceptually our main contribution is a general approach to equivariant learning that consolidates various constructions from many application areas into a common framework (Section 2 ). We make this approach practical with a user-friendly Python package . The user declares the input and output representations, the feature degree cutoffs, the coefficient functions, and the training data; the package computes minimal homogeneous generators and fits the resulting equivariant model in a few lines of code. In particular, the coefficient fitting functions can be any PyTorch module or any estimator with fit and predict methods, such as those in scikit-learn. Our package has built-in support for SO ⁡ ( 2 ) \operatorname{SO}(2) , O ⁡ ( 2 ) \operatorname{O}(2) , SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \operatorname{SO}(3) , O ⁡ ( 3 ) \operatorname{O}(3) , and 𝔖 n \mathfrak{S}_{n} , and it accepts other groups provided that the required representation-theoretic data are supplied. The resulting equivariant models can be viewed as end-to-end predictors, or as layerwise components in larger architectures. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 shows how existing equivariant learning models instantiate the general framework. Section 3 develops our algorithm for computing minimal homogeneous invariant and covariant generators up to prescribed degrees. Section 4 applies the algorithm to various groups and compares it with Gordan’s algorithm for SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \operatorname{SO}(3) . Section 5 demonstrates the full learning pipeline on the water Hamiltonian prediction problem and the EGNN benchmark. These show the model used as an end-to-end predictor and within layers of larger architectures, respectively. Section 6 summarizes our contributions and outlines future directions. items.raw_text: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators Michael Liaofan Liu † † thanks: Email: michael.liu.2024@utexas.edu Affiliation: Oden Institute, University of Texas at Austin Joe Kileel Affiliation: Oden Institute, University of Texas at Austin Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Texas at Austin Abstract We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite-dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures. 1 Introduction Many physical systems obey natural symmetries which learned models should respect. For example, changing coordinates in a system of charged particles should affect predicted accelerations according to the change of coordinates, while leaving predicted energies unchanged. Such transformation laws appear throughout science and engineering, and should constrain the class of admissible models. Equivariance formalizes this requirement. Let G G be a group acting on an input space X X and an output space Y Y . In data-driven applications we seek to learn a function F : X → Y F:X\to Y that is G G -equivariant , meaning that F ⁡ ( g ⋅ x ) = g ⋅ F ⁡ ( x ) F(g\cdot x)=g\cdot F(x) for all g ∈ G g\in G and x ∈ X x\in X , i.e., transforming the input and then predicting gives the same result as predicting and then transforming the output. When the action on Y Y leaves every output unchanged, this condition reduces to G G -invariance . A wide variety of approaches exist to encourage or enforce equivariance in machine learning models. For instance, data augmentation [ 48 , 10 ] encourages equivariance by training the model on many transformed copies of input-output pairs, but it does not guarantee equivariance in general. Equivariant multilayer perceptrons [ 20 ] enforce equivariance by solving linear constraints derived from group generators to parameterize equivariant linear layers. Equivariant graph networks [ 53 , 43 ] enforce equivariance through message passing. We investigate an alternative approach that enforces equivariance through polynomial features [ 36 , 59 , 56 ] . The underlying model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomials, called covariants , where the scalar coefficients are arbitrary learned functions of invariant polynomials, called invariants . To formalize this approach, suppose that X X and Y Y are finite-dimensional semisimple real G G -representations [ 21 ] . Suppose first that the target function F F is a polynomial. Then F F lies in the covariant module ℳ ⁡ ( X , Y ) ≔ { G -equivariant polynomial maps from ​ X ​ to ​ Y } . \mathcal{M}(X,Y)\coloneq\{\text{$G$-equivariant polynomial maps from }X\text{ to }Y\}. This is a module over the invariant algebra ℛ ⁡ ( X ) ≔ { G -invariant polynomials from ​ X ​ to ​ ℝ } , \mathcal{R}(X)\coloneq\{\text{$G$-invariant polynomials from }X\text{ to }\mathbb{R}\}, which is an algebra over ℝ \mathbb{R} . By Hilbert’s finiteness theorem (see Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 ), there exist finite generating sets { r 1 , … , r R } \{r_{1},\dots,r_{R}\} for ℛ ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{R}(X) as an ℝ \mathbb{R} -algebra and { m 1 , … , m M } \{m_{1},\dots,m_{M}\} for ℳ ⁡ ( X , Y ) \mathcal{M}(X,Y) as an ℛ ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{R}(X) -module. Thus, there exists a polynomial map p : ℝ R → ℝ M p\colon\mathbb{R}^{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} such that F ⁡ ( x ) = ∑ i = 1 M p i ​ ( r 1 ​ ( x ) , … , r R ​ ( x ) ) ​ m i ​ ( x ) . F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{M}p_{i}(r_{1}(x),\dots,r_{R}(x))m_{i}(x). (1) For arbitrary targets F F , we propose to replace the polynomial p p with a learnable function 𝒩 θ : ℝ R → ℝ M \mathcal{N}_{\theta}\colon\mathbb{R}^{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} , such as a neural network, a random forest, or a kernel regression model. This yields a class of G G -equivariant functions F θ ​ ( x ) = ∑ i = 1 M 𝒩 θ , i ​ ( r 1 ​ ( x ) , … , r R ​ ( x ) ) ​ m i ​ ( x ) , F_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathcal{N}_{\theta,i}(r_{1}(x),\dots,r_{R}(x))m_{i}(x), (2) where the goal is to learn θ \theta so that F θ ≈ F F_{\theta}\approx F . The ansatz can serve as an end-to-end predictor or as an equivariant component within a larger architecture. This model class has appeared before in various forms often under the name of “scalarization” [ 59 , 56 , 6 , 61 , 32 ] , but to our knowledge it has not yet been developed at our level of generality and packaged into a user-friendly toolkit. The work [ 32 ] precedes this one and is most similar. After introducing Eq. As an example, when G = O ⁡ ( d ) G=\operatorname{O}(d) , X = n ​ ℝ d X=n\mathbb{R}^{d} , and Y = ℝ d Y=\mathbb{R}^{d} , the invariant algebra is generated by the pairwise inner products x i ⋅ x j x_{i}\cdot x_{j} , and the covariant module is generated by the coordinate projections ( x 1 , … , x n ) ↦ x j (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\mapsto x_{j} [ 56 , Lemma 1 and Proposition 4] . When G = SO ⁡ ( 3 ) G=\operatorname{SO}(3) , Gordan’s algorithm or more modern variants can be used to compute the generators up to a given degree [ 38 , 32 ] . The e3nn [ 22 ] and lie-nn [ 3 ] packages can be used to compute explicit vector space bases for the homogeneous components of the covariant module and invariant algebra for various groups. One can then apply the graded Nakayama lemma to extract minimal homogeneous generators from these bases. One of our technical contributions is an alternative construction of vector space bases (Theorem 3.4 ) that uses the Cauchy decomposition to factor spaces tracking the action of G G from spaces tracking identical copies of irreducible representations in the input representation. This results in an algorithm (Algorithm 3.9 ) to compute minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and covariant module up to prescribed degrees. We also introduce data structures based on tensor networks to enable efficient storage and evaluation of the invariant and covariant features (Definition 3.5 ). Our method achieves large speedups (Figures 6 and 7 ) compared to a Gordan’s algorithm baseline for SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \operatorname{SO}(3) . Conceptually our main contribution is a general approach to equivariant learning that consolidates various constructions from many application areas into a common framework (Section 2 ). We make this approach practical with a user-friendly Python package . The user declares the input and output representations, the feature degree cutoffs, the coefficient functions, and the training data; the package computes minimal homogeneous generators and fits the resulting equivariant model in a few lines of code. In particular, the coefficient fitting functions can be any PyTorch module or any estimator with fit and predict methods, such as those in scikit-learn. Our package has built-in support for SO ⁡ ( 2 ) \operatorname{SO}(2) , O ⁡ ( 2 ) \operatorname{O}(2) , SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \operatorname{SO}(3) , O ⁡ ( 3 ) \operatorname{O}(3) , and 𝔖 n \mathfrak{S}_{n} , and it accepts other groups provided that the required representation-theoretic data are supplied. The resulting equivariant models can be viewed as end-to-end predictors, or as layerwise components in larger architectures. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 shows how existing equivariant learning models instantiate the general framework. Section 3 develops our algorithm for computing minimal homogeneous invariant and covariant generators up to prescribed degrees. Section 4 applies the algorithm to various groups and compares it with Gordan’s algorithm for SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \operatorname{SO}(3) . Section 5 demonstrates the full learning pipeline on the water Hamiltonian prediction problem and the EGNN benchmark. These show the model used as an end-to-end predictor and within layers of larger architectures, respectively. Section 6 summarizes our contributions and outlines future directions. items.summary: Alignment Oct 27, 2026 How AI agents shape experts‚Äô judgment calls As AI does more of the hands-on work, the hope is that experts still make the judgment calls, meaning the decisions with more than one defensible answer. We tested this with 50 professional analysts who did a statistical analysis with Claude Code. On each key decision, we randomly assigned which of two defensible options the agent would favor. Analysts mostly went with the agent‚Äôs side, and few named the agent as a reason afterward.

items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details Rational Transductors Mehryar Mohri ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract Standard Transformers excel at semantic modeling but struggle with rigid sequential logic and state tracking, fundamentally limited to AC0 complexity without intermediate chain-of- thought. In this work, we introduce Rational Transductors, a dual-stream architecture that augments the Transformer with a linear, matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA). By injecting rational state information into the attention mechanism via a Deep Rational Injection scheme, our framework strictly generalizes the expressive power of Transformers to capture all Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems (such as Parity and Modular Counting) while preserving O(log T) parallel training efficiency. View details Distributional Alignment Games for Answer-Level Fine-Tuning Mehryar Mohri Jon Schneider Yifan Wu ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract We focus on the problem of \emph{Answer-Level Fine-Tuning} (ALFT), where the goal is to optimize a language model based on the correctness or properties of its final answers, rather than the specific reasoning traces used to produce them. Directly optimizing answer-level objectives is computationally intractable due to the need to marginalize over the vast space of latent reasoning paths. To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a \emph{Distributional Alignment Game}. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. items.raw_text: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details Rational Transductors Mehryar Mohri ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract Standard Transformers excel at semantic modeling but struggle with rigid sequential logic and state tracking, fundamentally limited to AC0 complexity without intermediate chain-of- thought. In this work, we introduce Rational Transductors, a dual-stream architecture that augments the Transformer with a linear, matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA). By injecting rational state information into the attention mechanism via a Deep Rational Injection scheme, our framework strictly generalizes the expressive power of Transformers to capture all Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems (such as Parity and Modular Counting) while preserving O(log T) parallel training efficiency. View details Distributional Alignment Games for Answer-Level Fine-Tuning Mehryar Mohri Jon Schneider Yifan Wu ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract We focus on the problem of \emph{Answer-Level Fine-Tuning} (ALFT), where the goal is to optimize a language model based on the correctness or properties of its final answers, rather than the specific reasoning traces used to produce them. Directly optimizing answer-level objectives is computationally intractable due to the need to marginalize over the vast space of latent reasoning paths. To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a \emph{Distributional Alignment Game}. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. items.title: Commission preliminarily finds Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act for failure to tackle the sale of illegal products
items.summary: The European Commission preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to put in place reasonable, proportionate and effective measures to mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform. The Commission preliminarily found that Temu's mitigation measures include ineffective controls to check the compliance of products; a weak content moderation system; and an ineffective sanction system. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said: Shopping online should not mean risking the purchase of illegal and unsafe products. Under the Digital Services Act, platforms are responsible for protecting users from the risk of illegal content and goods. The preliminary findings against Temu mark another step towards making the online world safer. items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. Across Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B models, Vera Rubin NVL72 achieves 5x to 10x higher throughput per kilowatt and 3x to 5x higher end-to-end interactivity at matched concurrency compared with GB300 NVL72. NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, Tensor Cores, and sixth-generation NVLink to support agentic inference demands. Context-aware serving techniques including prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing reduce redundant computation and balance serving load across agentic workloads. Model-specific GPU execution optimizations such as DeepSeek's MegaMoE kernel and Qwen's multi-token prediction with Tensor Core verification reduce data movement and sequential decoding steps. Next Steps Read the companion blog post for more on NVIDIA training and inference performance. Visit MLPerf Endpoints results to review the published benchmark data. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Agentic workloads are demanding more from inference systems. AI agents carry growing conversation histories across turns and generate a mix of reasoning, tool calls, and responses. Inference systems must support users at scale while remaining responsive. MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 evaluates this balance between serving capacity and responsiveness using coding and enterprise workflows through API endpoints. During performance runs, generated tool calls and workflow intent are checked against reference values. Separate SWE-bench Verified evaluations assess end-to-end task-solving capability. These checks evaluate whether faster serving preserves model quality. In MLPerf Endpoints v1.0, provisional NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 results show over 10x the throughput per kilowatt of provisioned power of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user. 1 This post presents the benchmark results and outlines the hardware and software optimizations used in the submissions. 1 MLPerf® Endpoints v1.0, Kimi K3, Standardized division, Available category, published November 9, 2026. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, 32 accelerators, result 1.0.1.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1p, run 9: concurrency = 1,024 queries, TTFT P90 = 4,673.9 ms, system TPS = 41,414.2 tokens/sec, E2E average interactivity = 50.4 tokens/sec per user, operating power = 100.89 kW. NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, 48 accelerators, result 1.0.0.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1, run 6: concurrency = 48 queries, TTFT P90 = 2,305.1 ms, system TPS = 2,210.4 tokens/sec, E2E average interactivity = 56.2 tokens/sec per user, operating power = 60 kW. Comparison based on throughput per kilowatt at a shared minimum E2E average interactivity of 50 tokens/sec per user. Retrieved from endpoints.mlcommons.org on November 9, 2026. GB300 results verified by MLCommons Association. For the provisional Vera Rubin results: pending MLCommons Association verification, results are subject to change pending peer review. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. The serving demands of multi-turn agentic AI The MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 dataset captures these workload characteristics: coding trajectories accumulate history over many turns, while enterprise workflows reuse shared instructions, tool definitions, and business rules. Figure 1 shows how context length grows across model responses during extended agentic sessions. Figure 1. Context length grows across model responses in the MLPerf agentic dataset Vera Rubin delivers over 10x the agentic throughput per kilowatt The submissions span Kimi K3, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Table 1 compares provisional Vera Rubin NVL72 results with verified NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 results for throughput per provisioned kilowatt at a shared minimum end-to-end (E2E) interactivity threshold and for E2E interactivity at matched query concurrency. The curves show how much throughput each system delivers at a given responsiveness requirement. The step-function plot does not interpolate between measured points to keep comparisons grounded in demonstrated performance rather than estimates. Figure 2. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 throughput per provisioned kilowatt versus E2E interactivity on Kimi K3 in MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 Higher throughput per kilowatt enables organizations to run more agents simultaneously within the same power budget while meeting the same responsiveness requirement. At low concurrency, faster responses reduce inference wait times for latency-sensitive agentic tasks. Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores , and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions. Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. Efficient serving must preserve reusable state, distribute requests across workers, and accommodate the different execution requirements of prompt processing and token generation. Prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing help reduce redundant computation and balance serving load, while disaggregated serving supports independent optimization of prefill and decode. Figure 3 summarizes how context-aware serving and model-specific GPU execution support agentic inference. Figure 3. Context-aware serving and optimized GPU execution for agentic inference Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B also have distinct architectures that benefit from targeted GPU execution improvements. Model-specific kernels, fusion, optimized memory access, and speculative verification reduce data movement and execution overhead. Table 2 summarizes how these serving and execution techniques work together across the three models. Optimization How it improves performance Context reuse and routing Reuse previously processed conversation state and distribute requests to reduce recomputation and balance worker load. Example: Qwen’s fine-grained prefix matching reuses previously processed history across turns. Prefill and decode optimization Configure prompt processing and token generation independently through disaggregated serving, reducing contention and synchronization waits. Example: Kimi combines disaggregated serving with prefill changes that reduce GPU synchronization waits. Model-specific GPU execution Tailor kernels, fusion, and memory access to each architecture, reducing kernel launches and data movement. Example: DeepSeek’s MegaMoE kernel uses Rubin GPU locality and matrix-multiply instructions. Speculative generation and verification Propose multiple tokens and verify them together, reducing sequential decoding steps. Example: Qwen’s multi-token prediction pairs token proposals with Tensor Core verification. Table 2. Software optimizations improve context reuse, serving efficiency, and GPU execution More productive infrastructure for agentic AI Agentic inference performance depends on co-design across hardware, system architecture, and serving software. The provisional MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 results show how the Vera Rubin platform brings these capabilities together to address the demands of agentic workloads and create more capacity to serve users and scale applications. Learn more about NVIDIA training and inference performance in the companion blog post . Before working on MLPerf, he worked on TensorRT autonomous safety libraries and infrastructure, and NVIDIA CPU architecture modeling. Zhihan holds a master’s degree in Electrical Engineering from Stanford University, and a bachelor’s degree in Computer Engineering from Georgia Tech. Previously, she held product marketing and business development roles at C3 AI and IBM. She holds an MBA from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration from the Haas School of Business at the University of California, Berkeley. Verify important information. Learn more As AI agents tackle increasingly complex workflows, reducing time-to-train is critical for rapidly iterating on both models and the agents they power. MLPerf Training v6.1 marks the debut of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture, and these early results demonstrate that its CUDA software stack is already highly mature. NVIDIA swept all seven benchmarks, with the Vera Rubin NVL72 platform delivering the fastest time to train on six of the seven, achieving up to 2x more performance than a highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 baseline. For the seventh benchmark, DeepSeek-V3 671B, NVIDIA captured the absolute fastest time of the round by demonstrating massive scale on a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster. This dual-platform approach deliberately showcases the strengths of both systems. While the GB300 results highlight the massive, reliable cluster scale NVIDIA is deploying today, Vera Rubin demonstrated its own exceptional scaling architecture by maintaining above 97% overall efficiency when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs. Together, NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every benchmark in v6.1. NVIDIA platforms were also the only ones to submit results across all seven benchmarks, with Vera Rubin successfully completing the entire suite in its inaugural run. For developers, this breadth matters as much as any single top-line number. It proves that the performance gains inherited on day one span the entire modeling pipeline, comprehensively supporting everything from large-scale pretraining to the reinforcement learning post-training required for modern AI agents. Comprehensive AI performance across all MLPerf training benchmarks The simplest way to read this round is per benchmark: How much more performance does the new platform deliver per GPU on the same model? Vera Rubin NVL72 performance relative to GB300 NVL72 at the same GPU count on all seven MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmarks MLPerfTraining v6.1 results retrieved from www.mlcommons.org on Nov 16, 2026, from the following entries: 6.1-0116 , 6.1-0030, 6.1-0135, 6.1-0020, 6.1-0049, 6.1-0123, 6.1-0138, 6.1-0073, 6.1-0124, 6.1-0129 and 6.1-0038. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. The pattern is clear. The largest gain lands on the largest, most communication-heavy model. While the platform is consistently 1.4x to 1.6x faster across the rest of the suite, the generational advantage widens even further for the massive DeepSeek-V3 benchmark. The suite covers natural language, image generation, recommendation, and reinforcement learning, so the gains hold across multiple modalities as well as across different model shapes and architectures. DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload DeepSeek-V3 671B is a 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and the most demanding workload in the suite. Expert parallelism turns every iteration into a burst of all-to-all communication, so fabric efficiency shows up directly in time to train. Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks. GB300 NVL72 ran the identical 1,024-GPU configuration in 8.03 minutes, close to 2x per GPU, and the largest generational improvement in this round. Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality. At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack. Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark , Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding. The continuous cycle of generating rollouts, scoring them, and updating weights pushes system architectures to their limits by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines. Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved the fastest time for this new benchmark with a time of 10.44 minutes at 1,024 GPUs (6.1-0117), compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 (6.1-0031) at the same scale. The Vera Rubin platform also proved its flexibility by submitting on two different inference backends: NVIDIA NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM at 10.44 minutes and with vLLM at 10.94 minutes (6.1-0118). Shipping two viable inference backends on a benchmark this new says as much about software maturity as it does about silicon. Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act requires running each rollout in a simulated environment and executing tool calls, code, or API validations. Because driving these simulations is intensely CPU-bound, the NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture , sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack. While the GPUs handle massive token generation and rapid weight updates, the Vera CPUs work in lockstep to simulate the environments, ensuring the accelerators are continuously fed with the rich feedback required to perfect agentic workflows. NVLink, Quantum-X and Spectrum-X: Co-designed networking for high-efficiency AI scaling Every result above is also a networking result. Modern AI training requires thousands of processors to act as one, a challenge NVIDIA solves by co-designing the internal rack domain and the external cluster fabric. Inside the rack, Vera Rubin NVL72 connects 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs through a copper NVLink 6 spine. Delivering 3.6 TB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s per rack, this all-to-all domain keeps MoE expert dispatch off the critical path. Beyond the rack, the platform scales out via ConnectX-9 SuperNICs over Quantum-X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet. To manage bursty MoE traffic, both fabrics use adaptive routing and congestion control to keep all-to-all communications hidden behind the compute layer. This cohesive design translates directly to efficiency. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved above 97% scaling efficiency as it scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs (4 to 16 racks). GB300 NVL72 showcased the platform’s large-scale capabilities , extending to 10,240 GPUs to capture the fastest absolute result of the round. Because the NVL72 architecture provides a consistent 72-GPU domain, developers see predictable performance jumps every generation without altering their operating model. Each cycle simply delivers more compute and bandwidth across the same consistent fabric. Figure 2. Three generations of NVL72 systems at an identical 1,024-GPU scale MLPerfTraining v6.1 results retrieved from www.mlcommons.org on Nov 16, 2026, from the following entries: 6.1-0045, 6.1-0030 and 6.1-0116. Ratios are rounded. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. Continuous software optimization: Unlocking faster pretraining without hardware upgrades Vera Rubin’s results came from the NVIDIA AI software stack that customers receive: NVIDIA NeMo Framework 26.09 for the pretraining benchmarks, NVIDIA NeMo RL for the reinforcement learning benchmark, and NVIDIA PyTorch releases for FLUX.1 and DLRMv4. The optimizations are the ones described in our MLPerf Training v6.0 round . The stack also keeps moving after a round closes. Since v6.1 submissions were finalized, we have re-run several of the benchmarks on the same hardware and configuration with a newer software build. These are unverified results rather than MLCommons submissions, and we are sharing them because they show how continuous optimizations make NVIDIA infrastructure highly productive, durable, and fungible. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. That is what a mature software stack means for customers. The infrastructure gets faster after it ships, and the improvements continue to arrive, extending the platform’s productive lifetime and revenue generating potential. Because the CUDA platform is highly programmable, customers can unlock even more performance on their own. For example, Thinking Machines Lab developed an NVFP4 training recipe and custom kernels for its Inkling 2 Small model on GB300 NVL72, using NVFP4 for forward-pass MoE GEMMs and MXFP8 for gradients. Compared with full MXFP8 training, it sped up pretraining and fine-tuning by 8% and reinforcement learning by 20%, with minimal accuracy impact. An ecosystem that shipped on day one Vera Rubin’s debut in MLPerf Training v6.1 proves the architecture is built for immediate global deployment. With 80 percent of all closed-division submissions running on NVIDIA platforms across 20 partner organizations, these benchmarks represent reproducible performance across clouds and OEMs rather than isolated laboratory peaks. Systems are already generally available across various cloud infrastructure partners, complementing a multitude of AI Factory deployments around the globe. Today, Vera Rubin leads on performance per GPU across all seven workloads, while Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra maintain the scale record. Azure’s 2,560-node, 10,240-GPU GB200 NVL72 submission tied the NVIDIA 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 run to claim this round’s largest clusters. Partners are also pushing the limits of the architecture at the node level: Firmus used AI-driven kernel generation, with automated performance testing and mathematical validation, to post the fastest GB300 8-GPU result of the round, training GPT-OSS 20B in 52.90 minutes (6.1-0091) and Llama 3.1 8B in 52.40 minutes (6.1-0094). Because these platforms share a continuously optimizing CUDA software stack, developers can expect these inaugural metrics to climb steadily higher before the next MLPerf round even begins. As the Vera Rubin software stack matures the way the Blackwell stack did, expect these initial performance advantages to continue to unlock even greater value throughout the platform’s lifecycle. Prior to NVIDIA, Farshad held technical roles at leading semiconductor and consulting companies, where he helped build and manage large-scale generative AI and MLOps platforms for top technology customers.
