items.content: Simulation / Modeling / Design Build Training-Ready Physical AI Datasets with Two Prompts in NVIDIA Cosmos Curate, augment, generate, and label physical AI data, orchestrated by your coding agent. Nov 18, 2026 By Nakul Arora Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Cosmos is an open platform of frontier models, datasets, frameworks, and skills for world model development. NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory (CDF) provides five cloud-native blueprints and six composable skills to accelerate data curation, processing, and synthetic data generation for physical AI. The CDF Orchestration core skill coordinates workflow steps, deploys required services, and manages execution on a cluster for all five reference blueprints. Five training data use cases include generating driving scenarios for autonomous vehicle training, augmenting image attributes for search and re-identification, augmenting videos across weather and lighting, generating rare event videos, and generating defect images for visual inspection. Core agent skills such as Auto Labeling, AnomalyGen, Augmentation, Curation and Retrieval, Simulation, and Orchestration can be used independently or combined to build custom workflows. NVIDIA measured daily throughput on a cloud server with eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series GPUs, reporting up to 60x faster dataset assembly and 45x cheaper autonomous vehicle scenario generation compared to traditional methods. Next Steps Explore the NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory blueprints and composable skills to accelerate data curation and synthetic data generation. Watch the Build Training-Ready Datasets in Two Prompts livestream to learn how to curate and augment datasets for autonomous vehicles, robotics, and vision AI agents. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more World model accuracy starts with high-quality, diverse training datasets. Yet capturing rare defects, nighttime incidents, and other challenging scenarios is costly and time-consuming. Turning raw data into training-ready datasets adds complexity, particularly when using disconnected tools and manual processes for curation, labeling, generation, and evaluation. NVIDIA technology is helping developers more easily build high-quality, diverse training datasets at scale for physical AI . NVIDIA Cosmos is an open platform of frontier models , datasets, frameworks, and skills for world model development. As part of this platform, NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory (CDF) is a collection of five cloud-native blueprints and six composable skills to accelerate data curation, processing, and synthetic data generation (SDG) . Frontier AI agents can be used to orchestrate these blueprints, enabling prompt-to-data without human steering. This post walks you through how to curate and augment datasets or create anomalous events for physical AI model training with just two prompts in Cosmos. It features five different use cases. Video 1. Learn how to use a coding agent to turn a single warehouse image into labeled synthetic fall-event videos—with just a few prompts Set up and configure Cosmos blueprints and skills: Prompt 1 Cosmos Data Factory contains five reference blueprints for common tasks. All five blueprints run using the CDF Orchestration core skill , which coordinates workflow steps, deploys the required services, and manages execution on your cluster. To set it up, enter the following prompt into your coding agent: Example prompt: “Clone the CDF Orchestration repository, then run orchestration preflight and setup.” Preflight checks your environment without making changes and flags anything missing. Once those checks pass, setup prepares your environment to run the blueprints. Run the blueprint for your training data use case: Prompt 2 This section features five training data use cases for running the blueprint, including example prompts: Generate driving scenarios for autonomous vehicle (AV) training Augment image attributes for search and re-identification Augment videos across weather, lighting, and environments Generate rare event videos for model training Generate defect images for visual inspection If you already have footage or images and need to curate and add more variety, the first use case in this section covers generating driving scenarios, varying clothing attributes in person images, and transforming videos across weather, lighting, and environmental conditions. The augmentation use cases expand the variety in your existing data, but some training gaps call for creating entirely new events or defects. Your model might need to recognize a leaking product or a defective circuit board, but your dataset may contain few examples or none. Waiting to capture enough rare cases can take years, and staging them can be dangerous or expensive. The last two use cases cover generating rare event videos and defect images from images or 3D assets to fill these gaps. Use case 1: Generate driving scenarios for AV training The Autonomous Vehicle Dataset Generation blueprint helps you search large databases of driving scenarios and generate novel datasets for downstream model training and validation tasks. NVIDIA Cosmos Curator extracts metadata for your video dataset inputs, and NVIDIA Cosmos Dataset Search finds relevant videos through those embeddings. The retrieved videos are passed to NVIDIA Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video style transfer, and Cosmos Evaluator checks the generated videos for physical plausibility. Example prompt: “Search for driving scenes similar to our input video.mp4, transform them into rainy, snowy, and foggy while preserving layout and motion, and check physical plausibility.​” Figure 1. An AI agent orchestrates AV dataset generation, augmenting driving scenes with varied weather and lighting and checking physical plausibility Use case 2: Augment image attributes for search and re-identification The Image Attribute Augmentation reference blueprint generates variations of person-crops with controlled attribute changes such as clothing type, accessories, and color. An LLM turns your selected attributes into structured modification prompts, used to generate the augmented variations of the source image. Cosmos Evaluator confirms that the requested clothing attributes appear. The blueprint then auto-labels the results with clothing attributes and search queries for person search and re-identification. Example prompt: “Augment the person crops in <input-bucket>, three clothing variants per person, and write the output to <output-bucket>.” Figure 2. An AI agent generates outfit variations in images of people, verifies garment consistency, and annotates clothing attributes Use case 3: Augment videos across weather, lighting, and environments The Video Data Augmentation reference blueprint transforms your existing footage across weather, lighting, and environmental conditions while preserving scene structure. A vision lang uage model ( VLM) describes your source video and combines that with your requested conditions into a structured prompt, which Cosmos3-Nano uses to generate the augmented variant. Cosmos Evaluator checks each generated clip for motion artifacts that aren’t in your source, confirms that the conditions you asked for actually appear, and scores whether the motion is physically plausible. Next, the blueprint auto-labels both your source and generated videos with detection, tracking, and captions. It then provides you with a training-ready dataset. Example prompt: “Run video data augmentation on the videos in <input-bucket>, create 3 augmentations for yellow lighting, dim lighting and red table. Write the output to <output-bucket>.” Figure 3. An AI agent orchestrates visual variations of a robot-manipulation scene, changing lighting and tabletop appearance while checking physical plausibility Use case 4: Generate rare event videos for model training The Event Video Generation reference blueprint uses a source image to create videos of rare events, such as fires, falls, or shoplifting. A VLM combines its description of your scene with your requested event into a structured prompt. Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video generates the clip while preserving the source viewpoint and layout. Cosmos Evaluator checks whether the event appears and whether motion looks physically plausible, retrying failed clips. Passing clips are auto-labeled with detections, tracks, captions, and semantic annotations for downstream training. Example prompt: “Run the Event Video Generation blueprint on the image in <input-bucket> to generate 3 clips: normal traffic, stalled vehicle, and collision at the intersection. Write the output to <output-bucket>.” Figure 4. An AI agent orchestrates retail event generation from a grocery store scene, producing floor-level spills, falling boxes, and shelf smoke, followed by quality review and annotation Use case 5: Generate defect images for visual inspection The Defect Image Generation reference blueprint creates defective examples from clean inspection images or 3D USD assets of parts such as circuit boards, glass panels, or metal surfaces. For 3D assets, NVIDIA Isaac Sim renders inspection images and masks, and Qwen-Image-Edit creates realistic clean reference images, called golden images. Cosmos 3 Super uses these images, defect masks, and your requested defect types to generate defects while preserving the surrounding part. It ships fine-tuned for printed circuit boards (PCBs), glass, and metal, with further fine-tuning skills available for other use cases. You get golden images, synthetic defect images, and manifests tracing each result to its source and generation settings. Example prompt: “Run the Defect Image Generation blueprint and generate shift structural defects for images in <input-bucket> with full board coverage. Write the output to <output-bucket>.” Figure 5. An AI agent orchestrates PCB defect-data preparation, selecting USD board assets for component-rotation defects and real inspection images for excess-solder examples How to u se core agent skills and tools for specific tasks like curation, search, and labeling The blueprints outlined in the previous section are built from six core agent skills : Auto Labeling , AnomalyGen , Augmentation , Curation and Retrieval , Simulation , and Orchestration . You can use these skills independently or combine them to build a workflow around your own data and goals. Auto Labeling: Turns raw video and images into annotated datasets with detection, tracking, captions and scene understanding. AnomalyGen : Creates realistic defect images from a handful of examples, with masks, for visual inspection. Augmentation : Generates visual variations of your video and images using Cosmos models, for conditions you can’t capture. Curation and Retrieval : Finds clips and images in a large collection, using Cosmos Curator and Cosmos Dataset Search. Simulation: Renders photorealistic, fully labeled images from 3D scenes using Isaac Sim and Omniverse Replicator. Orchestration : Runs reference blueprints on your cluster, deploying the services each one needs and scaling them. Example prompt: Clone the auto labeling repo https://github.com/NVIDIA/cdf-auto-labeling/tree/main . Perform video auto-labeling to label my videos at <input-bucket>. Save outputs to <output-bucket>. Use the locally deployed model at <endpoint> for VLM and LLM. Figure 6. An AI agent orchestrates video labeling through object tracking, dense captioning, visual question answering, and reasoning For workflows focused on curation and retrieval, use Cosmos Curator to process and auto-label raw video and multimodal data, and Cosmos Dataset Search to find targeted training scenarios across large datasets. Cosmos Curator now supports multicamera video, IMU, and GPS inputs, plus initial lidar support in its sensor library. Reusable Python processing components and Managed Ray on Slurm orchestration help teams connect sensor observations, test curation strategies, and use spare GPU capacity. Planned expansion includes additional lidar devices, radar, and other sensor types. Cosmos Dataset Search, now open source under the Apache 2.0 license, combines metadata, scene semantics, spatial relationships, and temporal behavior through multi-embedding retrieval and adaptive agentic reranking (early access). Its modular APIs and agent skills retrieve relevant video segments for training datasets or the augmentation blueprints above. Generate t raining data up to 60x f aster and 45 x c heaper Cosmos Data Factory skills and blueprints turn hard-to-collect training data into a compute workload you control. The NVIDIA team measured daily throughput on a cloud server with eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series GPUs at roughly $40 per server-hour, or $960 per day, then divided daily cost by output to estimate cost per asset. A V d ataset g eneration: Generates ~130 edge-case clips/day at $2.66 in GPU compute per clip, about 45x cheaper than a fleet crew costing $125 per scenario collected on the road. Image attribute augmentation: Augments ~42,649 annotated image pairs/day at $960/day, or $0.023 per pair, about 10x cheaper than the $0.25 average for third-party purchased data. Video data augmentation: Augments ~305 annotated clips/day at $3.15 per ~5-minute clip, about 7x cheaper than the $22 average we’ve paid for third-party data. Defect i mage g eneration: Dropped dataset assembly time from two months to one day, a 60x speedup. Event video generation: Generates ~384 annotated clips/day at $2.50 each and ~4 minutes per clip, creating scarce training examples of fires, fights, and falls without waiting for or recreating dangerous real incidents. With Cosmos, training gaps become generation jobs with a measurable compute budget. Note that these figures cover compute only; source data preparation, setup, agent use, storage, and human review may add costs. What results and projected outcomes are organizations reporting with Cosmos? Several organizations are using Cosmos skills and blueprints to improve testing, detection, and search accuracy across autonomous vehicles, visual inspection, and robotics while targeting lower costs and effort. Improving recall on real-world anomalies by up to 24% with synthetic data and estimated 1,400x return on data-generation cost at an offshore oil and gas site. Targeting up to 85% less manual engineering effort in automated optical inspection (AOI) program generation – with 40% fewer false calls . Reducing repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shortening AI regression test cycles by up to 85% (expected). Going to market in under two weeks with Cosmos Curator compared to an estimated six months (time required to build an equivalent pipeline in-house). Get started with NVIDIA Cosmos To accelerate data curation, processing, and synthetic data generation for your application, check out NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory blueprints and composable skills. Start with a blueprint that matches your use case, follow the setup guide, and use your AI agent to run the workflow with your data. Customize your pipeline with individual skills to generate high-quality, annotated training datasets. To learn more, join us on November 19 for the livestream, Build Training-Ready Datasets in Two Prompts . Learn how to use Cosmos to curate and augment datasets for AVs, robotics, and vision AI agents. Featuring Voxel51 and Encord, the livestream will highlight how Porsche uses Cosmos Data Factory through the Voxel51 platform and how Encord worked with ANYbotics. He drives product strategy across NVIDIA's three-computer architecture–from synthetic data generation and simulation to training and real-world inference at the edge and cloud–turning physical infrastructure into intelligent, responsive systems. For 3D assets, NVIDIA Isaac Sim renders inspection images and masks, and Qwen-Image-Edit creates realistic clean reference images, called golden images. Cosmos 3 Super uses these images, defect masks, and your requested defect types to generate defects while preserving the surrounding part. It ships fine-tuned for printed circuit boards (PCBs), glass, and metal, with further fine-tuning skills available for other use cases. You get golden images, synthetic defect images, and manifests tracing each result to its source and generation settings. Example prompt: “Run the Defect Image Generation blueprint and generate shift structural defects for images in <input-bucket> with full board coverage. Write the output to <output-bucket>.” Figure 5. An AI agent orchestrates PCB defect-data preparation, selecting USD board assets for component-rotation defects and real inspection images for excess-solder examples How to u se core agent skills and tools for specific tasks like curation, search, and labeling The blueprints outlined in the previous section are built from six core agent skills : Auto Labeling , AnomalyGen , Augmentation , Curation and Retrieval , Simulation , and Orchestration . You can use these skills independently or combine them to build a workflow around your own data and goals. Auto Labeling: Turns raw video and images into annotated datasets with detection, tracking, captions and scene understanding. AnomalyGen : Creates realistic defect images from a handful of examples, with masks, for visual inspection. Augmentation : Generates visual variations of your video and images using Cosmos models, for conditions you can’t capture. Curation and Retrieval : Finds clips and images in a large collection, using Cosmos Curator and Cosmos Dataset Search. Simulation: Renders photorealistic, fully labeled images from 3D scenes using Isaac Sim and Omniverse Replicator. Orchestration : Runs reference blueprints on your cluster, deploying the services each one needs and scaling them. Example prompt: Clone the auto labeling repo https://github.com/NVIDIA/cdf-auto-labeling/tree/main . Perform video auto-labeling to label my videos at <input-bucket>. Save outputs to <output-bucket>. Use the locally deployed model at <endpoint> for VLM and LLM. Figure 6. An AI agent orchestrates video labeling through object tracking, dense captioning, visual question answering, and reasoning For workflows focused on curation and retrieval, use Cosmos Curator to process and auto-label raw video and multimodal data, and Cosmos Dataset Search to find targeted training scenarios across large datasets. Cosmos Curator now supports multicamera video, IMU, and GPS inputs, plus initial lidar support in its sensor library. Reusable Python processing components and Managed Ray on Slurm orchestration help teams connect sensor observations, test curation strategies, and use spare GPU capacity. Planned expansion includes additional lidar devices, radar, and other sensor types. Cosmos Dataset Search, now open source under the Apache 2.0 license, combines metadata, scene semantics, spatial relationships, and temporal behavior through multi-embedding retrieval and adaptive agentic reranking (early access). Its modular APIs and agent skills retrieve relevant video segments for training datasets or the augmentation blueprints above. Generate t raining data up to 60x f aster and 45 x c heaper Cosmos Data Factory skills and blueprints turn hard-to-collect training data into a compute workload you control. The NVIDIA team measured daily throughput on a cloud server with eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series GPUs at roughly $40 per server-hour, or $960 per day, then divided daily cost by output to estimate cost per asset. A V d ataset g eneration: Generates ~130 edge-case clips/day at $2.66 in GPU compute per clip, about 45x cheaper than a fleet crew costing $125 per scenario collected on the road. Image attribute augmentation: Augments ~42,649 annotated image pairs/day at $960/day, or $0.023 per pair, about 10x cheaper than the $0.25 average for third-party purchased data. Video data augmentation: Augments ~305 annotated clips/day at $3.15 per ~5-minute clip, about 7x cheaper than the $22 average we’ve paid for third-party data. Defect i mage g eneration: Dropped dataset assembly time from two months to one day, a 60x speedup. Event video generation: Generates ~384 annotated clips/day at $2.50 each and ~4 minutes per clip, creating scarce training examples of fires, fights, and falls without waiting for or recreating dangerous real incidents. With Cosmos, training gaps become generation jobs with a measurable compute budget. Note that these figures cover compute only; source data preparation, setup, agent use, storage, and human review may add costs. What results and projected outcomes are organizations reporting with Cosmos? Several organizations are using Cosmos skills and blueprints to improve testing, detection, and search accuracy across autonomous vehicles, visual inspection, and robotics while targeting lower costs and effort. Improving recall on real-world anomalies by up to 24% with synthetic data and estimated 1,400x return on data-generation cost at an offshore oil and gas site. Targeting up to 85% less manual engineering effort in automated optical inspection (AOI) program generation – with 40% fewer false calls . Reducing repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shortening AI regression test cycles by up to 85% (expected). Going to market in under two weeks with Cosmos Curator compared to an estimated six months (time required to build an equivalent pipeline in-house). Get started with NVIDIA Cosmos To accelerate data curation, processing, and synthetic data generation for your application, check out NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory blueprints and composable skills. Start with a blueprint that matches your use case, follow the setup guide, and use your AI agent to run the workflow with your data. Customize your pipeline with individual skills to generate high-quality, annotated training datasets. To learn more, join us on November 19 for the livestream, Build Training-Ready Datasets in Two Prompts . Learn how to use Cosmos to curate and augment datasets for AVs, robotics, and vision AI agents. Featuring Voxel51 and Encord, the livestream will highlight how Porsche uses Cosmos Data Factory through the Voxel51 platform and how Encord worked with ANYbotics. items.content: Back to Articles BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model Team Article Published November 11, 2026 Upvote 33 +27 Milan Gritta milangritta Follow qvac Jihye Back happy-jihye Follow qvac JinUk, Cho jucho2725 Follow qvac ohjoon kwon joooon Follow qvac Patrik Lambert patrik-lambert Follow qvac Mathias Buus mafintosh Follow qvac Amril Nurman Nurman Follow qvac Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. 🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4) Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead. Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages. Copyright Complaints We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. Key Highlights Benchmark results Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets). Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives. Methodology BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3). Figure 3: BotPsy training recipe. The student goes through four stages. Three specialist Qwen3.5-4B teachers, each RL-trained for one skill, guide it during the distillation stage. Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards. Learning from demonstrations (SFT) We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called. Learning from teachers (MOPD) Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4). Figure 4: Mean score of each capability group after each training stage. SFT boosts tool use but pushes knowledge and instruction following below the base model; distillation brings both back above base, and the RL stages add further gains on all three. Learning from rules and environments (RL stages) Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth. The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling. Data composition Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use. Figure 5: Approximate training-data composition per stage, grouped by capability. Results Tool use & agents BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5). Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× BFCL v4¹ 44.0 23.4 37.7 28.1 22.8 ACEBench² 58.7 30.1 55.4 39.4 24.5 τ-bench³ 51.5 23.2 46.5 6.5 28.8 Claw-Eval⁴ 46.5 39.3 48.9 31.6 31.0 BrowseComp-Plus⁵ 4.5 1.9 2.8 0.2 0.8 ToolSandbox⁶ 64.6 30.5 41.2 45.7 28.1 Average 45.0 24.7 38.8 25.3 22.7 Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined ; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Knowledge Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× GPQA Diamond⁷ 38.1 33.2 59.9 35.0 15.8 MMLU-Pro⁸ 48.9 41.6 65.5 39.4 40.0 Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Instruction following BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× IFEval⁹ 90.8 59.7 80.0 85.6 78.4 IFBench⁹ 55.9 22.0 40.9 33.9 40.6 Multi-IF¹⁰ 67.2 43.2 66.9 68.2 53.4 Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Multi-turn conversations The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1). Figure 6: Multi-turn agentic tasks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, ACEBench Agent, τ²-bench (retail, telecom) and τ³-bench (banking). BotPsy leads four of the five benchmarks; on τ³-banking, every model stays below 5. Weak spots BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8). Where it works: app-level performance breakdown BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ. Single tool calls work well everywhere Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70). Figure 7: Mean per-scenario score (0–100, higher is better) by app group, for simple (left) and complex (right) scenarios. n gives the number of simple / complex scenarios in each group; the bottom row is the unweighted mean of the seven groups. The largest gains are in multi-step tasks On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks. Multi-step information retrieval is the weak spot Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14). Inference efficiency BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer. Figure 8: Accuracy against reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench. Tokens are measured on questions all five models answer correctly; accuracy is over all questions. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each. Figure 9: Pass rate against assistant turns per solved task on τ²-bench retail and telecom. Turns are measured on tasks all five models solve; pass rate is over all tasks. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9): τ²-retail: 10.7 turns, against 11.7 for the base (9% fewer) and 10.6 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. τ²-telecom: 13.1 turns, against 17.6 for the base (26% fewer) and 13.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think (5% fewer). It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks. Intended Use and Limitations BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty . BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics. items.raw_text: Back to Articles BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model Team Article Published November 11, 2026 Upvote 33 +27 Milan Gritta milangritta Follow qvac Jihye Back happy-jihye Follow qvac JinUk, Cho jucho2725 Follow qvac ohjoon kwon joooon Follow qvac Patrik Lambert patrik-lambert Follow qvac Mathias Buus mafintosh Follow qvac Amril Nurman Nurman Follow qvac Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. 🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4) Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead. Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages. Copyright Complaints We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. Key Highlights Benchmark results Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets). Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives. Methodology BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3). Figure 3: BotPsy training recipe. The student goes through four stages. Three specialist Qwen3.5-4B teachers, each RL-trained for one skill, guide it during the distillation stage. Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards. Learning from demonstrations (SFT) We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called. Learning from teachers (MOPD) Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4). Figure 4: Mean score of each capability group after each training stage. SFT boosts tool use but pushes knowledge and instruction following below the base model; distillation brings both back above base, and the RL stages add further gains on all three. Learning from rules and environments (RL stages) Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth. The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling. Data composition Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use. Figure 5: Approximate training-data composition per stage, grouped by capability. Results Tool use & agents BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5). Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× BFCL v4¹ 44.0 23.4 37.7 28.1 22.8 ACEBench² 58.7 30.1 55.4 39.4 24.5 τ-bench³ 51.5 23.2 46.5 6.5 28.8 Claw-Eval⁴ 46.5 39.3 48.9 31.6 31.0 BrowseComp-Plus⁵ 4.5 1.9 2.8 0.2 0.8 ToolSandbox⁶ 64.6 30.5 41.2 45.7 28.1 Average 45.0 24.7 38.8 25.3 22.7 Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined ; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Knowledge Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× GPQA Diamond⁷ 38.1 33.2 59.9 35.0 15.8 MMLU-Pro⁸ 48.9 41.6 65.5 39.4 40.0 Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Instruction following BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× IFEval⁹ 90.8 59.7 80.0 85.6 78.4 IFBench⁹ 55.9 22.0 40.9 33.9 40.6 Multi-IF¹⁰ 67.2 43.2 66.9 68.2 53.4 Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Multi-turn conversations The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1). Figure 6: Multi-turn agentic tasks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, ACEBench Agent, τ²-bench (retail, telecom) and τ³-bench (banking). BotPsy leads four of the five benchmarks; on τ³-banking, every model stays below 5. Weak spots BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8). Where it works: app-level performance breakdown BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ. Single tool calls work well everywhere Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70). Figure 7: Mean per-scenario score (0–100, higher is better) by app group, for simple (left) and complex (right) scenarios. n gives the number of simple / complex scenarios in each group; the bottom row is the unweighted mean of the seven groups. The largest gains are in multi-step tasks On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks. Multi-step information retrieval is the weak spot Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14). Inference efficiency BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer. Figure 8: Accuracy against reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench. Tokens are measured on questions all five models answer correctly; accuracy is over all questions. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each. Figure 9: Pass rate against assistant turns per solved task on τ²-bench retail and telecom. Turns are measured on tasks all five models solve; pass rate is over all tasks. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9): τ²-retail: 10.7 turns, against 11.7 for the base (9% fewer) and 10.6 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. τ²-telecom: 13.1 turns, against 17.6 for the base (26% fewer) and 13.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think (5% fewer). It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty . BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics. items.content: Back to Articles Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models Published November 11, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 36 +30 Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors! Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget. In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4 , my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring. With pool_factor=4 , a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold , the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved. Pooling at inference Mean vectors Ordinary model Pooling-aware model Gain (points) Unpooled 193.22 51.84 52.39 +0.55 pool_factor=2 96.86 50.10 51.74 +1.64 pool_factor=3 64.74 49.70 51.45 +1.76 pool_factor=4 48.68 49.03 51.23 +2.20 pool_factor=5 39.04 48.13 50.28 +2.15 pool_factor=6 32.62 47.07 49.85 +2.78 max_tokens=64 54.76 49.27 50.89 +1.63 max_tokens=32 29.58 48.25 50.12 +1.87 max_tokens=16 15.60 46.61 49.26 +2.65 max_tokens=8 7.99 43.12 46.61 +3.48 max_tokens=4 4.00 37.22 43.00 +5.78 distance_threshold (calibrated) 54.76 50.10 51.24 +1.14 distance_threshold (calibrated) 29.58 48.38 50.96 +2.58 distance_threshold (calibrated) 15.60 47.23 49.63 +2.41 For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps. At the trained pool_factor=4 , nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39. The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget. Combining Compression Techniques If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order: Embedding quantization to 4, 2, or 1 bit(s), for example via Fast-PLAID , to reduce storage per coordinate. Token pooling to reduce the number of document vectors, optionally with pooling-aware fine-tuning as shown in this blog. Matryoshka token embeddings to reduce the dimensionality of each token vector, optionally with fine-tuning to preserve retrieval quality at smaller widths. If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus. MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings. Try the complete training example , choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model. With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical! References Stefan Josef. Learn to Pool: Lightweight Fine-Tuning for Flexible Multi-Vector Compression .
