items.content: Back to Articles The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Published November 12, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 44 +38 Suvaditya Mukherjee suvadityamuk Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository . If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works . Let’s go! Introduction 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. What we want to improve A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. What will we use? LoRA LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have: A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain from here Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3 , because DINOv3 is a gated model If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start. How TRELLIS.2 works Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. Encoding the input image First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage. O-Voxel and Structured Latents O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer. Geometry Generation (Shape Flow) The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512. We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape. Material Generation + Mesh Creation In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures. Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file. Planning Which components to fine-tune We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities. Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training. If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Why use LoRA Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more. What you’ll run A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning. To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub: Give the containers access to your data. Set the parameters for your task. Run the preprocessing container. Run the fine-tuning container. Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training. Experiment overview We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment: Prepare the data. Convert GLB or OBJ meshes into the latent representations TRELLIS.2 uses for training, and render the input images. Train the adapters. Run one job for each DiT, with the prepared dataset and a LoRA configuration. Explain the code. Examine how the containers load the data, add adapters, and train the models. We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it. Walkthrough Running on Hugging Face Jobs Preprocessing The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline . See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository . export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 6h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep \ --meshes your-username/my-meshes \ --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --private --holdout 0.05 \ --views 16 --workers 8 For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments: flag meaning -d Detach: print the job ID and URL, then return. To follow the job, run hf jobs logs -f <id> --flavor a100-large The hardware. We use a100-large (80 GB). To see all options, run hf jobs hardware --timeout 6h The job stops after this time. Both commands resume. Preprocessing skips finished objects. Training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to --secrets HF_TOKEN Send your token (from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login) to the job as an encrypted environment variable. The token is not written into the image cr.hf.co/...:latest The image to run. All text after it is the command that runs in the container This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here . The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later. LoRA Fine-tuning The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run. We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 If you set --push-to , the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity . A compact script is also available in the same repository . If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have , feel free to use the following set of commands. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For the Shape Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Running locally with Docker Preprocessing The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different. # For preprocessing into latents docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep --meshes your-username/my-meshes --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 LoRA Fine-tuning # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands: export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso Inside the training pipeline Preprocessing into latents We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again. We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training. Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train ( ss or shape ), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning. cfg = json.load( open ( { "ss" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/ss_flow_lora_gso.json" , "shape" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json" , }[FLOW] ) ) key, latents = { "ss" : ( "ss_latent" , "ss_latents/ss_enc_conv3d_16l8_fp16_64" ), "shape" : ( "shape_latent" , "shape_latents/shape_enc_next_dc_f16c32_fp16_512" ), }[FLOW] roots = json.dumps( { "gso" : { key: f" {DATA} / {latents} " , "render_cond" : f" {DATA} /renders_cond" , "meta" : DATA, } } ) ds = getattr (datasets, cfg[ "dataset" ])(roots, **cfg[ "dataset_args" ]) holdout = set ( open ( f" {DATA} /holdout.txt" ).read().split()) ds.instances = [(root, sha) for root, sha in ds.instances if sha not in holdout] batches = cycle( DataLoader( ds, batch_size=BATCH, shuffle= True , drop_last= True , num_workers= 4 , collate_fn= getattr (ds, "collate_fn" , None ), ) ) Preparing LoRA adapters We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model() . This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface. We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point ( fp32 ) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 ( bf16 ) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. model = models.from_pretrained(cfg[ "ckpt" ]) for block in model.blocks: block.use_checkpoint = True inject_adapter_in_model( LoraConfig( r=cfg[ "rank" ], lora_alpha=cfg[ "alpha" ], target_modules=cfg[ "lora_targets" ] ), model, ) params = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): p.requires_grad_( "lora_" in name) if p.requires_grad: p.data = p.data. float () # fp32 master weights for LoRA params.append(p) model.cuda().train() Training It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3 , Flux 2 , and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching. We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen. The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands. We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. opt = torch.optim.AdamW( params, lr=cfg[ "lr" ], weight_decay=cfg[ "weight_decay" ], betas=( 0.9 , 0.95 ) ) dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor( cfg[ "image_cond_model" ], image_size=cfg[ "image_size" ] ).cuda() We then follow these steps within the training loop: Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config). Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting. Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise). Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions. Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t ). def flow_loss ( x0, cond ): s = cfg[ "t_schedule" ] t = ( torch.rand(x0.shape[ 0 ]) if s[ "name" ] == "uniform" else torch.sigmoid( torch.randn(x0.shape[ 0 ]) * s[ "args" ][ "std" ] + s[ "args" ][ "mean" ] ) ) t = t.cuda() noise = ( x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats)) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else torch.randn_like(x0) ) tv = t.view(- 1 , *[ 1 ] * ( len (x0.shape) - 1 )) x_t = ( 1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg[ "sigma_min" ] + ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * tv) * noise pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000 , cond), ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * noise - x0 return ( F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else F.mse_loss(pred, target) ) The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches. For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps. for step in range ( 1 , STEPS + 1 ): for _ in range (ACCUM): batch = next (batches) x0 = recursive_to_device(batch[ "x_0" ], "cuda" ) with torch.no_grad(): cond = dino(batch[ "cond" ]) cond[torch.rand( len (cond), device= "cuda" ) < cfg[ "p_uncond" ]] = 0 with torch.autocast( "cuda" , dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg[ "grad_clip" ]) opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Results We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours. The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry. Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects. The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans. We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set: Metric What it means Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better. F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better. Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better. In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects. For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space . Future directions Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate job
items.raw_text: Back to Articles The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Published November 12, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 44 +38 Suvaditya Mukherjee suvadityamuk Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository . If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works . Let’s go! Introduction 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. What we want to improve A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. What will we use? LoRA LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have: A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain from here Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3 , because DINOv3 is a gated model If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start. How TRELLIS.2 works Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. Encoding the input image First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage. O-Voxel and Structured Latents O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer. Geometry Generation (Shape Flow) The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512. We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape. Material Generation + Mesh Creation In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures. Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file. Planning Which components to fine-tune We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities. Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training. If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Why use LoRA Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more. What you’ll run A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning. To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub: Give the containers access to your data. Set the parameters for your task. Run the preprocessing container. Run the fine-tuning container. Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training. Experiment overview We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment: Prepare the data. Convert GLB or OBJ meshes into the latent representations TRELLIS.2 uses for training, and render the input images. Train the adapters. Run one job for each DiT, with the prepared dataset and a LoRA configuration. Explain the code. Examine how the containers load the data, add adapters, and train the models. We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it. Walkthrough Running on Hugging Face Jobs Preprocessing The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline . See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository . export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 6h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep \ --meshes your-username/my-meshes \ --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --private --holdout 0.05 \ --views 16 --workers 8 For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments: flag meaning -d Detach: print the job ID and URL, then return. To follow the job, run hf jobs logs -f <id> --flavor a100-large The hardware. We use a100-large (80 GB). To see all options, run hf jobs hardware --timeout 6h The job stops after this time. Both commands resume. Preprocessing skips finished objects. Training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to --secrets HF_TOKEN Send your token (from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login) to the job as an encrypted environment variable. The token is not written into the image cr.hf.co/...:latest The image to run. All text after it is the command that runs in the container This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here . The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later. LoRA Fine-tuning The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run. We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 If you set --push-to , the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity . A compact script is also available in the same repository . If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have , feel free to use the following set of commands. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For the Shape Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Running locally with Docker Preprocessing The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different. # For preprocessing into latents docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep --meshes your-username/my-meshes --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 LoRA Fine-tuning # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands: export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso Inside the training pipeline Preprocessing into latents We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again. We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training. Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train ( ss or shape ), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning. cfg = json.load( open ( { "ss" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/ss_flow_lora_gso.json" , "shape" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json" , }[FLOW] ) ) key, latents = { "ss" : ( "ss_latent" , "ss_latents/ss_enc_conv3d_16l8_fp16_64" ), "shape" : ( "shape_latent" , "shape_latents/shape_enc_next_dc_f16c32_fp16_512" ), }[FLOW] roots = json.dumps( { "gso" : { key: f" {DATA} / {latents} " , "render_cond" : f" {DATA} /renders_cond" , "meta" : DATA, } } ) ds = getattr (datasets, cfg[ "dataset" ])(roots, **cfg[ "dataset_args" ]) holdout = set ( open ( f" {DATA} /holdout.txt" ).read().split()) ds.instances = [(root, sha) for root, sha in ds.instances if sha not in holdout] batches = cycle( DataLoader( ds, batch_size=BATCH, shuffle= True , drop_last= True , num_workers= 4 , collate_fn= getattr (ds, "collate_fn" , None ), ) ) Preparing LoRA adapters We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model() . This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface. We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point ( fp32 ) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 ( bf16 ) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. model = models.from_pretrained(cfg[ "ckpt" ]) for block in model.blocks: block.use_checkpoint = True inject_adapter_in_model( LoraConfig( r=cfg[ "rank" ], lora_alpha=cfg[ "alpha" ], target_modules=cfg[ "lora_targets" ] ), model, ) params = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): p.requires_grad_( "lora_" in name) if p.requires_grad: p.data = p.data. float () # fp32 master weights for LoRA params.append(p) model.cuda().train() Training It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3 , Flux 2 , and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching. We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen. The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands. We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. opt = torch.optim.AdamW( params, lr=cfg[ "lr" ], weight_decay=cfg[ "weight_decay" ], betas=( 0.9 , 0.95 ) ) dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor( cfg[ "image_cond_model" ], image_size=cfg[ "image_size" ] ).cuda() We then follow these steps within the training loop: Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config). Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting. Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise). Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions. Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t ). def flow_loss ( x0, cond ): s = cfg[ "t_schedule" ] t = ( torch.rand(x0.shape[ 0 ]) if s[ "name" ] == "uniform" else torch.sigmoid( torch.randn(x0.shape[ 0 ]) * s[ "args" ][ "std" ] + s[ "args" ][ "mean" ] ) ) t = t.cuda() noise = ( x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats)) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else torch.randn_like(x0) ) tv = t.view(- 1 , *[ 1 ] * ( len (x0.shape) - 1 )) x_t = ( 1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg[ "sigma_min" ] + ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * tv) * noise pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000 , cond), ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * noise - x0 return ( F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else F.mse_loss(pred, target) ) The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches. For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps. for step in range ( 1 , STEPS + 1 ): for _ in range (ACCUM): batch = next (batches) x0 = recursive_to_device(batch[ "x_0" ], "cuda" ) with torch.no_grad(): cond = dino(batch[ "cond" ]) cond[torch.rand( len (cond), device= "cuda" ) < cfg[ "p_uncond" ]] = 0 with torch.autocast( "cuda" , dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg[ "grad_clip" ]) opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Results We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours. The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry. Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects. The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans. We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set: Metric What it means Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better. F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better. Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better. In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects. For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space . Future directions Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate job

items.content: Back to Articles Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run Published November 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 98 +92 Célina Hanouti celinah Follow Victor Mustar victor Follow Bertrand Chevrier kramp Follow Lucain Pouget Wauplin Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Eliott Coyac coyotte508 Follow Julien Chaumond julien-c Follow Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Routing powered by OpenRouter OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. items.content: Back to Articles DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency Team Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 10 +4 Jason Chen jzsc Follow RadixArk Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0 : BF16 FP8 NVFP4 The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. Run DaisyRose-27B We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url= "http://localhost:30000/v1" , api_key= "none" , ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model= "DaisyRose-27B" , messages=[ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "How many positive divisors does 360 have?" , } ], temperature= 1.0 , top_p= 0.95 , extra_body={ "top_k" : 20 , "min_p" : 0.0 }, ) print (response.choices[ 0 ].message.reasoning_content) print (response.choices[ 0 ].message.content) The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . Benchmark results Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B DaisyRose-27B Terminal Bench 4.1 5.6 12.0 Terminal Bench 2.1 73.0 75.5 DeepSWE v1.1 42.2 46.2 SWE Bench Pro v2 91.3 94.7 HLE (text-only) 33.9 34.3 IFBench 79.5 82.4 GPQA Diamond 89.2 90.7 DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. High-quality training data We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. We selected tasks using three criteria: Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran Qwen3.8-27B on every task and redesigned each one around the mistakes we wanted the model to stop making. We then adjusted the difficulty until the solve rate fell within a useful learning range. Each task requires several interdependent steps. The agent has to reason, plan, and execute across a long job. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox, with more than 100 tool calls and more than 256K output tokens. Tasks must reward actually solving the problem. We reviewed every task alongside the model’s attempts. Tasks that could be passed without solving the intended problem, or that contained a design flaw, were fixed or removed. Efficient training backend RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization. 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash. 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs. Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady. Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs. Robust sandbox service Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently . The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%. Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine. Try the model or train your own Download DaisyRose-27B , follow the SGLang serving guide , or use Miles to train your own agents. We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab. We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor. Adapted from the original RadixArk article . items.content: Back to Articles Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases Enterprise Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 18 +12 Nicholas Fuller nfuller Follow ibm-research Sean Falconer thefalc Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Bilge Zeren Aksu bzeren Follow ibm-research Julian Payne Pyjamacardinal Follow ibm-research Mountu Jinwala mjinwala Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Chandra Reddy creddyhf Follow ibm-research Vijay Ekambaram vijaye12 Follow ibm-research Arindam Jati ajati Follow ibm-research Robert Metzger rmetzger0 Follow ibm-research Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy ( documentation ). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.( documentation ). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs. The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made. See how time series and real-time context come together to create value: Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening. A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state. Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere. Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate. Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them. This approach can help teams in four ways: - Scale model development . A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one. - Refresh predictions as data changes . Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration. - Put signals closer to decisions . Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment. - Run compact models on CPUs. items.content: Back to Articles 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 7 +1 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . What is Strata? Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Engine Decode (tok/s) Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88 llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64 llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1 vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3 Transformers + Accelerate 0.16 Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box. Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . Start small I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla. experts_offload I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 . To try it, install Transformers from that PR: pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head" Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: path = snapshot_download( "tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming" ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( f" {path} /dense" , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map={ "" : "mps" , "experts.*" : "disk" }, quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits= 8 ), experts_offload={ "cache_bytes" : 12 << 30 , "quantized_experts" : f" {path} /experts-q3" , }, ) That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script : the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table. Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout. The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option. Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward . It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Runs anywhere : native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code 40+ languages : automatic language detection Output control : numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language Extremely fast : an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches Holds up on real phone calls : on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark Quickstart Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers uv pip install torch transformers accelerate from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelF
items.content: Back to Articles Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 10 +4 Reson8 reson8-thomas Follow Reson8 Mark 't Hart MarktHart Follow Reson8 Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Runs anywhere : native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code 40+ languages : automatic language detection Output control : numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language Extremely fast : an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches Holds up on real phone calls : on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark Quickstart Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers uv pip install torch transformers accelerate from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request( audio= "https://hf.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/bcn_weather.mp3" , language= "English" , # omit to detect automatically ).to(model.device, dtype=model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 512 ) generated = output[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ]:] print (processor.decode(generated, return_format= "transcription_only" )[ 0 ]) # return_format="parsed" if detecting language audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these. How it's built Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code . To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip. On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities. On-policy distillation with GOLD Results Accuracy for its size On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER . The best score for its size Speed Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx . That's an hour of audio in about half a second. Real phone calls Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER , on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better. Real phone calls, 14 English accents Try it The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash . It's also available through our API . We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.24892 (cs) [Submitted on 18 Nov 2026] Title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents Authors: Hengguang Zhou , I-Hung Hsu , Li Chen , Priyanshi Shrivastava , Anastasios Angelopoulos , Wei-Lin Chiang , Ion Stoica , Cho-Jui Hsieh View a PDF of the paper titled On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents, by Hengguang Zhou and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.
