items.content: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents Hengguang Zhou I-Hung Hsu Li Chen Priyanshi Shrivastava Anastasios Angelopoulos Wei-Lin Chiang Ion Stoica Cho-Jui Hsieh Abstract User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5 ∼ \sim 6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users’ goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities. November 18, 2026 \ArenaTitleFont 1 UCLA 2 Arena \ArenaHeadingFont 1. \ArenaHeadingFont Introduction With the capability advances, LLM agents help users write code, create documents, and revise other artifacts ( Kimi Team, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2026 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) through multi-turn interactions ( Dou et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Baumann et al., 2026 ) . During these interactions, users clarify what they want, inspect the work produced, and provide feedback. Evaluating this process requires a user who can respond to the agent’s progress, but recruiting real users for every evaluation is costly and makes comparisons difficult to repeat. User simulators offer a practical way to run these interactions at scale and are used in both offline agent evaluation and training ( Barres et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ; Suh et al., 2026 ) . However, using simulated users in place of real users can change measured agent success rates ( Seshadri et al., 2026 ) . To assess whether simulators can reliably stand in for real users in multi-turn interactions, recent studies have developed several ways to evaluate user simulators, including similarity to human language and behavior, consistency with user specifications ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Jain and Sandhu, 2026 ) , and agreement with human assessments of agent performance ( Dou et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . What remains less clear is whether these measures reliably identify behavior that makes a simulator unsuitable for agent evaluation where artifacts deeply involved in the interaction. For example, a simulated user may sound natural while approving a broken artifact or overlooking an important requirement. Evaluating fidelity is also difficult because a replay should preserve the original user’s needs while responding to an agent whose actions may differ from the original session. We therefore need to examine how evaluation metrics respond when these aspects of simulation go wrong. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. Specifically, we introduce failures through controlled perturbations ( Sai et al., 2021 ) to the simulator’s setup, then replay each session with the assigned agent. We test whether the metrics assign lower scores to these perturbed replays than to controls generated from the same source sessions and agent assignments. We design 10 perturbations based on three sources of motivation. First, we draw on reported failure modes, including overly helpful simulated users ( Naous et al., 2026 ) , premature information disclosure ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Jain and Sandhu, 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , and self-preference in LLM evaluation ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ; Spiliopoulou et al., 2025 ) . Second, we draw on failures observed in our analysis of 442,516 real sessions and 20,100 replays. Third, we include basic defects that evaluation metrics should readily detect. These include changing the user’s goal, removing constraints, forcing early termination, encouraging acceptance of broken work, and favoring a selected agent. We ask whether the existing user simulator evaluation metrics penalize these changes and what replays are retained when using their score for filtering. The results reveal several gaps in the evaluation suites from SimulatorArena, VISTA, and SWE-Together ( Dou et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . We count a perturbation as detected if at least one metric in an evaluation suite shows a reliable score decrease relative to the control (Section 6.1.1 ). Under this criterion, the evaluation suites adapted from SimulatorArena, VISTA, and SWE-Together ( Dou et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) detect six, five, and six of the ten perturbations, respectively. All three evaluation suites fail to detect the agent favoritism perturbation (more favorable feedback from the simulated user toward a selected agent) despite the shifts it causes in agents’ scores and ranks. The composite scores for these metrics even favor perturbed replays that accept broken work. These findings suggest that high scores on existing criteria do not necessarily establish that a simulator provides useful feedback for help evaluating interactive agents. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a new evaluation suite that measures user simulators at three levels illustrated in Figure 2 . Downstream ranking agreement checks whether simulated interactions recover a supplied reference ranking of agents. This assesses the simulator’s utility for agent evaluation, but gives limited information about why it succeeds or fails. We therefore also measure population-level fidelity , which compares collective interaction patterns with those of real users, and trace-level fidelity , which checks whether each replay preserves the user’s goals, constraints, and persona. The two fidelity levels help distinguish broad behavior shifts from failures within individual sessions. Together, these measures provide a stronger and more holistic assessment of how well a simulator supports agent evaluation at a broader range of failures than any of the existing benchmarks we evaluated. We show that our evaluation suite detects all ten tested perturbations under the same criterion in Sec 6.1 . We also test whether our evaluation scores can help filtering out simulator failures. We report the fraction of control traces retained at a threshold that admits 5% of perturbed samples. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5 ∼ \sim 6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users’ goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities. November 18, 2026 \ArenaTitleFont 1 UCLA 2 Arena \ArenaHeadingFont 1. \ArenaHeadingFont Introduction With the capability advances, LLM agents help users write code, create documents, and revise other artifacts ( Kimi Team, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2026 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) through multi-turn interactions ( Dou et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Baumann et al., 2026 ) . During these interactions, users clarify what they want, inspect the work produced, and provide feedback. Evaluating this process requires a user who can respond to the agent’s progress, but recruiting real users for every evaluation is costly and makes comparisons difficult to repeat. User simulators offer a practical way to run these interactions at scale and are used in both offline agent evaluation and training ( Barres et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ; Suh et al., 2026 ) . However, using simulated users in place of real users can change measured agent success rates ( Seshadri et al., 2026 ) . To assess whether simulators can reliably stand in for real users in multi-turn interactions, recent studies have developed several ways to evaluate user simulators, including similarity to human language and behavior, consistency with user specifications ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Jain and Sandhu, 2026 ) , and agreement with human assessments of agent performance ( Dou et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . What remains less clear is whether these measures reliably identify behavior that makes a simulator unsuitable for agent evaluation where artifacts deeply involved in the interaction. For example, a simulated user may sound natural while approving a broken artifact or overlooking an important requirement. Evaluating fidelity is also difficult because a replay should preserve the original user’s needs while responding to an agent whose actions may differ from the original session. We therefore need to examine how evaluation metrics respond when these aspects of simulation go wrong. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. Specifically, we introduce failures through controlled perturbations ( Sai et al., 2021 ) to the simulator’s setup, then replay each session with the assigned agent. We test whether the metrics assign lower scores to these perturbed replays than to controls generated from the same source sessions and agent assignments. We design 10 perturbations based on three sources of motivation. First, we draw on reported failure modes, including overly helpful simulated users ( Naous et al., 2026 ) , premature information disclosure ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Jain and Sandhu, 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , and self-preference in LLM evaluation ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ; Spiliopoulou et al., 2025 ) . Second, we draw on failures observed in our analysis of 442,516 real sessions and 20,100 replays. Third, we include basic defects that evaluation metrics should readily detect. These include changing the user’s goal, removing constraints, forcing early termination, encouraging acceptance of broken work, and favoring a selected agent. We ask whether the existing user simulator evaluation metrics penalize these changes and what replays are retained when using their score for filtering. The results reveal several gaps in the evaluation suites from SimulatorArena, VISTA, and SWE-Together ( Dou et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . We count a perturbation as detected if at least one metric in an evaluation suite shows a reliable score decrease relative to the control (Section 6.1.1 ). Under this criterion, the evaluation suites adapted from SimulatorArena, VISTA, and SWE-Together ( Dou et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) detect six, five, and six of the ten perturbations, respectively. The composite scores for these metrics even favor perturbed replays that accept broken work. These findings suggest that high scores on existing criteria do not necessarily establish that a simulator provides useful feedback for help evaluating interactive agents. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a new evaluation suite that measures user simulators at three levels illustrated in Figure 2 . Downstream ranking agreement checks whether simulated interactions recover a supplied reference ranking of agents. This assesses the simulator’s utility for agent evaluation, but gives limited information about why it succeeds or fails. We therefore also measure population-level fidelity , which compares collective interaction patterns with those of real users, and trace-level fidelity , which checks whether each replay preserves the user’s goals, constraints, and persona. The two fidelity levels help distinguish broad behavior shifts from failures within individual sessions. Together, these measures provide a stronger and more holistic assessment of how well a simulator supports agent evaluation at a broader range of failures than any of the existing benchmarks we evaluated. Finally, we apply the evaluation suite to six simulators on 351 real sessions. None of the six simulators we evaluated leads across all three levels. The simulator from SimulatorArena achieves the highest downstream ranking agreement, while our proposed profile-based simulator lead on population-level and trace-level fidelity. These results show the value of examining all three levels when assessing a simulator. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.24891 (cs) [Submitted on 18 Nov 2026] Title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity Authors: Benjamin Novotny , Doug Szeto , Chang Wang , Shicheng Chen , George Zhihua Yuan , Bob Kamma , Michael Ge , John Xin Zhou , Andrea Olgiati View a PDF of the paper titled Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity, by Benjamin Novotny and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait. Correspondence to: Benjamin Novotny <benovo@meta.com>. Preprint. Abstract A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track , a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta’s traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend’s current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track . It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate’s refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait. 1 Introduction The traffic shaper is a shared internal dispatch service for online, asynchronous LLM inference in Meta’s social media applications, including post and per-minute live-video understanding. We study four of these workloads in depth, plus two that joined later (Section 6.4 ). Each day the shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and stages hundreds of terabytes of media. As load shifts, the shaper decides how much work each inference engine gets. The wrong amount leaves engines idle or overloaded. Accelerators and provider capacity are scarce and slow to add (Section 2 ), so both should stay busy. For an engine we run, busy means a full batch. Work waiting beyond what keeps that batch full adds only delay and timeouts. When the shaper and its hand-tuned precursor ran at their dispatch limits, the precursor kept its engines’ batches only about a third full (Section 6.3 ). Staged services, production overload controllers, and receiver-issued credits have long bounded waiting work Welsh et al. (2001) ; Zhou et al. (2018) ; Cho et al. (2020) . In LLM serving, demand and supply shift. Demand, the work callers send, swings in volume with daily cycles, events, and backfills (bulk jobs over existing content, launched at any time). Request size depends on an output length unknown a priori Kwon et al. (2023) and shifts with the token mix and reasoning length. Supply, the serving capacity behind a backend, moves as shared pools congest, replicas are preempted, and fleets resize. Continuous batching rewards concurrency Yu et al. (2022) . But past the throughput plateau, more concurrency only adds queueing delay and KV-cache pressure Kwon et al. (2023) . Prefill and decode stress different resources Zhong et al. (2024) ; Agrawal et al. (2024) . We measure capacity by goodput, the rate of requests completed within their timeout. Production stacks scatter admission across tiers. A provider’s admission refuses work. A gateway accepts work whenever it can take a connection. An engine queues sequences. Our design rule keeps unbounded waiting out of execution, so neither networks nor engines hold more work than they can serve. Each engine keeps a short queue behind its running batch. Everything else waits in FOQS , Meta’s durable priority queue. Cap , a lightweight, fail-fast admission check at the resource that saturates, surfaces overload as a refusal (HTTP 429), so the dispatcher need not predict request size. Providers already return such refusals. For internal engines, we enabled the model server’s per-replica cap, so total admission scales with the fleet (Section 4 ). vLLM 0.29, released after we deployed, adds a queue limit like that cap, off by default vLLM Project (2026) . A limit only refuses, so a short engine queue needs a dispatcher that follows the limit closely. A looser dispatcher needs a deeper queue, which exposes more in-flight work to timeouts and dropped connections (Section 7 ). Track is the close-following dispatcher, a dedicated dispatch loop per capacity domain (a provider quota domain or serving pool). Track learns the ceiling, the highest rate the backend currently serves, only from the Cap ’s refusals. The durable queue drains only at Track ’s rate. The shaper implements Cap-and-Track . The four main workloads, named by their capacity or model, all serve post and live-video understanding. The reserved and on-demand workloads run on matching provider capacity. The classifier and zero-shot workloads run a fine-tuned classifier and a zero-shot model on internal H100 and MI300X fleets. With the same Cap and Track , the shaper matched demand to capacity in the fixed reservation, the variable on-demand pool, and resized internal fleets. It needed no capacity retuning through nine fleet resizes and an elastic pool’s preemptions (Section 6.3 ). It worked alongside engine tuning (Section 7 ). Three workloads replaced precursors that queued work durably and, without Track , dispatched it with stateless jobs at a hand-set global rate. The reserved workload’s precursor, the static system, rode the same provider admission as the shaper and differed only in its dispatcher. In a pre-launch test, the shaper took over. Within two hours, refusals fell from about 23% to 3–5%, near the shaper’s 5% target. Refusals rose again when the static system resumed. At launch, the reservation’s unused capacity more than halved (observational). Since the provider updated its admission, the shaper’s utilization has averaged 95.8% of the reservation and 99.1% through a backlogged week (Section 4 ). For the classifier and zero-shot precursors, the global rate was in effect a Cap blind to engine state. In concurrent A/Bs on production traffic, the shaper, with a Cap at each engine and Track , served the classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its precursor. Under the shaper, lower-priority work waited longer at a backfill’s peak. On equal zero-shot fleets of about 600 MI300X each, the shaper drained every shared backlog first, by a median 3 hours. When both ran at their dispatch limits, the shaper’s engines ran a median 124 of 128 sequences, against the precursor’s 41, and served 9% more per GPU on prefill-heavy work (Section 6.3 ). In replay without a Cap , the engine stayed busy, but goodput fell to zero. At a stable ceiling, Track behind per-replica caps came within 1% of the goodput of a rate fixed 20% above measured capacity, with a refusal share about a quarter of the fixed rate’s (Sections 6.1 and 6.2 ). A well-tuned fixed rate can match or beat Track while the ceiling holds, but does not move with the ceiling. If the ceiling doubles, the fixed rate leaves half the capacity idle. If the ceiling halves, half its attempts are refused. The ceiling moves with fleet resizes, elastic-pool preemptions, and token-mix shifts. The precursors’ fixed rates were retuned by hand repeatedly. In production, Track has worked with four kinds of Cap : model-server caps, provider admission, a per-caller token quota in our gateway, and an engine queue-depth aware router. Cap-and-Track composes established mechanisms above a serving framework, using the framework’s per-replica limit as the Cap and adding the durable priority queue and refusal-driven fleet-level rate that serving frameworks lack. We make four contributions. We present an LLM dispatch design that composes durable priority waiting, fail-fast admission, and feedback-driven dispatch across provider and internal backends, so fleets can be sized for typical load instead of peak. Section 5 describes the engineering that makes a simple rule safe on a changing fleet: central placement on a consistent hash ring with hysteresis, one leader that pushes each worker its share of each queue’s rate, round-robin service across many queues per worker, drain and freeze through restarts, and runtime knobs for every constant. We report evidence at two levels, controlled replay on real engines (Sections 6.1 and 6.2 ) and production, including same-traffic A/Bs for two workloads (Section 6.3 ). Section 7 draws lessons: cap the engine’s queue, use the dispatcher to locate the ceiling, pick the Cap by its job, keep dispatch stateful, make the simple path the only path, and size the fleet for freshness. 2 Production Setting and Requirements Inference results feed downstream products under freshness goals set by priority, and no user waits on a request. Producers submit work through one enqueue interface. We study its online lane, and Appendix A.1 covers the batch lane. The traffic shaper serves three resource models. Reserved provider capacity is a fixed token allocation, and measured utilization can briefly exceed 100%. On-demand capacity varies because its quota caps consumption but reserves no hardware, and the provider’s other callers share the pool behind that quota. When that pool is congested, reachable capacity falls below quota and the provider sheds the excess with HTTP 429. Internal capacity is vLLM inference engines on H100, MI300X, and MI350X fleets, each wrapped by a custom model server. A replica is one engine (one H100 or two MI300X). The model server’s per-replica request cap decides which requests enter that replica. Another model runs on a fourth accelerator type in external data centers. Across the six workloads, fleets held more than 4,000 accelerators at their peaks, plus reserved provider capacity (Appendix A.1 ). We see a provider only through the 429s it returns for a capacity domain as a whole. Inside a serving pool, Cap refuses at each replica, and the pool admits the sum of its replicas’ caps. In production, callers sharing a capacity domain share one online queue and one dispatch rate. A tenant is a serving deployment on our platform, and an attempt is one dispatch, refused or not. Freshness is enqueue-to-result time, spanning queue wait and inference. The reserved, classifier, and zero-shot workloads had precursors, and we call the reserved workload’s precursor the static system. All three precursors ran stateless jobs on a serverless asynchronous job platform built on FOQS . Each job type had one global, hard-coded dispatch rate that engineers set and adjusted by hand. Failed requests retried independently, without feedback. Adding capacity is slow. A new replica takes a median of 136 s (classifier) to 159 s (zero-shot) to load its model and serve. The shaper’s control loop runs every 15 seconds. Even with GPU quota granted, two classifier resizes took 27 and 13 minutes from landing to serving, excluding review. They grew the fleet from 34 to 45 H100s (Appendix A.3 ). Cap-and-Track assumes work that can wait and backends that refuse promptly, with one controller per capacity domain. 3 Pitfalls Under Shifting Supply and Demand Dispatchers that back off on refusals, like Track , cope with shifting supply and demand (Section 8 ), unlike the designs below. Static limits. A fixed request rate protects a backend only for the workload mix used to choose it. A lighter mix strands capacity, and a heavier one overloads execution. A fixed rate cannot follow moving capacity. Token-aware limits help when token counts are known. But generative output length is unknown at admission. Even fine-tuned predictors estimate that length poorly Zhang et al. (2026) . Queues inside the server. Inference engines queue accepted work. By default, vLLM holds requests beyond its running batch in a waiting queue. Orca and vLLM improve how an engine schedules and stores sequences Yu et al. (2022) ; Kwon et al. (2023) . But neither decides how much asynchronous work waits inside the replica. A model server that limits concurrency by blocking callers adds a second, in-memory queue. Requests in either queue hold memory and connections while their deadlines run, without durable priority or redelivery. Across a fleet, each engine serves and times out its own line, in its own order. A request retried on timeout can land behind a longer line on another replica, so priority becomes best effort. Cap refuses instead of blocking. A refused request returns promptly to the head of its worker’s ready queue, outside the engine (Section 5 ). On lease expiry, the request returns to the shared priority queue, where backlog is visible and recoverable. Peak provisioning and autoscaling. Provisioning for an observed peak cannot cover an arbitrary backfill and holds accelerators for work that could wait. Over three months, serving mean classifier arrivals needed 25 H100s. The busiest hour reached 4.0 times that mean. Serving that hour on arrival would need at least 99 H100s (Appendix A.3 ). Autoscaling alone falls short. At the classifier’s sharpest one-hour rise, a fleet that reacts within an hour, without a queue, would need at least 74 more H100s than the preceding hour’s arrivals required. Capacity arrives late and leaves abruptly, in whole-replica steps (Section 3 and Appendix A.3 ). Reserved provider capacity cannot be autoscaled. 4 Cap-and-Track Design 4.1 Traffic shaper overview Producers enqueue work into FOQS (Figure 1 a). Track workers lease requests from FOQS , stage any input media, and dispatch through a gateway to an external provider or an internal model server. (a) System waiting execution Track control Cap Enqueue interface Batch queues Batch workers Online queues Online workers Track (MIMD) Gateway per-caller quota model server, cap per replica ⋯ \cdots cap vLLM cap vLLM engine queue-depth aware router router ⋯ \cdots vLLM vLLM External providers reserved, on-demand, batch API Response queues Response workers Datastore dispatch HTTP 429 batch results (b) Online worker pipeline, one worker FOQS Prefetch loop per queue (pauses on full ready queue) Buffers (per queue) media staging, pipelined In flight, 3 ​ N 3N (round robin) Downloads, N N at once Uploads, N N at once Ready queues (per queue) Dispatch loop (round robin, per-queue pacing) Gateway One leader: each queue’s rate 429: front of ready queue target rate polls fleet counters, 15 s Figure 1: The traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track . (a) One enqueue interface feeds online and batch queues. Track runs in the online workers and dispatches each queue through the gateway at its learned rate. A refusal from any of the four kinds of Cap (model-server cap, provider admission, per-caller quota, or engine queue-depth aware router) returns as HTTP 429. Other failures stay outside the feedback loop. (b) Each worker paces each queue at the rate the leader pushes. A 429 returns the request to the front of its ready queue with media staged. Up to 3 ​ N 3N media items are in flight, but only N N download and N N upload at once. The rest wait between the two stages to keep each worker container’s network bandwidth saturated. 4.2 Cap: fail fast near execution A labeled refusal at the constrained resource exposes overload before a wasteful wait, so the dispatcher needs no model of inference-engine internals or provider accounting. Providers already return such refusals as HTTP 429. The traffic shaper records each 429, slows dispatch, and keeps the work. Refusals use no reserved tokens. Internal serving produces the same signal. Before a request reaches vLLM, the model server checks the replica’s in-flight count and, at the cap, returns an overload exception that the RPC layer marks as an overload. The gateway maps only overload statuses to HTTP 429 (Appendix A.8 ). Without a refusal path, an engine queues work until timeout (Section 2 ), so each replica needed its own refusal. We enabled the model server’s existing per-replica cap and tied it to engine tuning. Our classifier and zero-shot deployments set vLLM’s max_num_seqs to 128 and the server’s request and processing caps to 140 per replica (together, “the cap”). This slight oversubscription keeps a few requests waiting in the model server or behind a nearly full batch, so a freed slot refills without a dispatcher round trip (Appendix A.4 ). Profiling sweeps engine settings to find a workload’s highest-throughput configuration, including the concurrency where throughput plateaus. Set the cap with the engine settings, from profiling or a standard deployment template for a token mix in a validated range. The cap needs no precise tuning. Correspondence to: Benjamin Novotny <benovo@meta.com>. Preprint. Abstract A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track , a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta’s traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend’s current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track . It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate’s refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait. 1 Introduction The traffic shaper is a shared internal dispatch service for online, asynchronous LLM inference in Meta’s social media applications, including post and per-minute live-video understanding. Accelerators and provider capacity are scarce and slow to add (Section 2 ), so both should stay busy. For an engine we run, busy means a full batch. Work waiting beyond what keeps that batch full adds only delay and timeouts. When the shaper and its hand-tuned precursor ran at their dispatch limits, the precursor kept its engines’ batches only about a third full (Section 6.3 ). Request size depends on an output length unknown a priori Kwon et al. (2023) and shifts with the token mix and reasoning length. Supply, the serving capacity behind a backend, moves as shared pools congest, replicas are preempted, and fleets resize. Continuous batching rewards concurrency Yu et al. (2022) . But past the throughput plateau, more concurrency only adds queueing delay and KV-cache pressure Kwon et al. (2023) . Prefill and decode stress different resources Zhong et al. (2024) ; Agrawal et al. (2024) . We measure capacity by goodput, the rate of requests completed within their timeout. Production stacks scatter admission across tiers. A provider’s admission refuses work. A gateway accepts work whenever it can take a connection. An engine queues sequences. Our design rule keeps unbounded waiting out of execution, so neither networks nor engines hold more work than they can serve. Each engine keeps a short queue behind its running batch. Everything else waits in FOQS , Meta’s durable priority queue. Cap , a lightweight, fail-fast admission check at the resource that saturates, surfaces overload as a refusal (HTTP 429), so the dispatcher need not predict request size. Providers already return such refusals. items.summary: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.24881 (cs) [Submitted on 18 Nov 2026] Title: Monoculture Robust Learning Authors: Lee Cohen , Jon Kleinberg , Omer Reingold View a PDF of the paper titled Monoculture Robust Learning, by Lee Cohen and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Monoculture Robust Learning Lee Cohen Affiliation: Stanford University Jon Kleinberg Affiliation: Cornell University Omer Reingold Affiliation: Stanford University Abstract We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture ( Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021 ) : the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output k k individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on k k independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness , and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all k k hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability ( Impagliazzo et al., 2022 ) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is ρ ho -replicable, then running it independently k k times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with k k , controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and ρ ho . We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to γ \gamma can require a sample-size multiplier of t = Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / γ ) ) t=\Omega(\log(1/\gamma)) . 1 Introduction In many real-world settings, people find themselves in situations where k k competing agents (or firms) offer the same type of opportunity or benefit, and each agent uses a learned decision rule to decide whether to extend an offer to a given individual. The individual may receive offers from multiple agents but ultimately accepts at most one. Examples include loan approvals across multiple banks, screening across multiple employers, ticket access for the same concert through different agencies, discounted travel offers during the holidays across competing platforms, or promotional discounts (e.g., a discounted haircut) across several salons in the same promotion network. If these agents rely on the same model, e.g., a single ad system that serves the ads for all the agents, their mistakes can become correlated, and the same individual can be rejected by all k k agents, even though the environment appears to provide multiple “chances.” This is the problem of algorithmic monoculture ( Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021 ) , in which the use of a common underlying model by multiple competing firms leads to correlated errors and consequently adverse consequences for individuals (and sometimes for the firms themselves). It is a common concern with modern machine learning systems, which are often deployed in settings where multiple providers use a common training pipeline and/or common dataset, and therefore their algorithms may repeatedly misclassify the same inputs . This means that even if an individual appears to be getting k k “tries” at an opportunity when they apply to k k different providers, they might in fact be getting something that more resembles a single try at the opportunity, since the misclassifications of all k k providers’ models are very similar. In this paper, we seek strategies to mitigate the negative effects of algorithmic monoculture, asking: if we only have access to one dataset, can we still produce k k accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is significantly lower than a single hypothesis? We formalize this question in the Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) setting by introducing individual monoculture robustness and its average analogue, expected monoculture robustness . We consider a learner that, given a single sample S ∼ 𝒟 n S\sim\mathcal{D}^{n} , outputs k k hypotheses h 1 , … , h k h_{1},\ldots,h_{k} , and measure monoculture failure via the conjunctive error : the event that all k k hypotheses misclassify a fixed point x x or, in expectation, a random point x ∼ 𝒟 X x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X} . This captures the “shared blind spot” that motivates monoculture concerns: beyond standard accuracy guarantees, it cares about the correlation of errors across the returned hypotheses, not just their marginal risks. This has a direct connection to algorithmic fairness ( Dwork et al., 2012 ) . Fairness and accuracy guarantees are typically stated for a single predictor, but in the settings above an individual effectively faces k k predictors in parallel (or over short time horizons), and what matters is the chance that all of them reject the individual. When errors are correlated across agents, “apply to more places” or “try another place” provides far less protection than one would expect under independence, and the harm can be concentrated on the same people or groups across many decision-makers. Monoculture robustness is designed to capture this concern by shifting attention from marginal error of each model to the joint failure probability across the k k models. A notable conceptual point is that monoculture failure can arise from two sources of randomness. Sometimes the error is sample-driven : for a point x x , most internal random seeds fail whenever the drawn sample is unrepresentative for x x . In this regime, rerunning the same algorithm on the same sample will not help much, and reducing the conjunctive error requires genuinely more data. Other times the error is internal randomness driven : for a typical sample S S , there are many seeds that predict the correct label, so rerunning with fresh randomness can reduce the probability that all k k runs land in the “bad” seeds. This separation guides our lower bound and the positive results. Throughout this work, we study both fundamental limits on monoculture robustness and concrete procedures for achieving it, including ERM-based and replicable learners. Contributions. Motivated by practical monoculture failures and the desire to “simulate” independence from a single dataset, we outline our contributions as follows. 1. Problem formulation. In section 2 , we formalize monoculture robustness for PAC learning by modeling a learner that, given a single dataset, outputs k k accurate hypotheses intended to serve k k agents. We quantify monoculture failure via conjunctive error and distinguish expected monoculture error from the stronger individual version. We also clarify when individual guarantees are meaningful, namely for a point x x with nontrivial single-run error of the base learning algorithm q x q_{x} (it is inherently uninformative to demand small joint failure when the single-run error is large). 2. Lower bounds and unavoidable sample increase . We show that, in the realizable setting, individual monoculture robustness cannot in general be improved beyond what additional independent data provides: there exist simple classes and an input x x for which driving the individual monoculture error at x x down to γ \gamma can require a sample-size multiplier t = Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / γ ) ) t=\Omega(\log(1/\gamma)) . In particular, for sample-driven failures, this sample-size increase is generally unavoidable. 3. Replicability and same-sample joint error reduction . In section 4 we analyze (pointwise) replicability ( Impagliazzo et al., 2022 ; Hopkins et al., 2025 ) as a black-box condition under which rerunning a learner independently k k times on the same sample provably helps: the individual monoculture error shrinks exponentially with k k , controlled by q x q_{x} and the replicability parameter. This section also makes two conceptual points: (i) Replicability might appear counterintuitive for achieving monoculture robustness. After all, replicability is a stability property where a learning algorithm produces w.h.p. the exact same hypothesis when trained on different samples, provided the internal randomness seed remains fixed. We show that it can still produce diversity across seeds on a fixed sample; and (ii) monoculture robustness is weaker than replicability, so while replicability provides individual monoculture robustness guarantees “for free”, it is useful only if we require replicability regardless. 4. Expected Monoculture Error. When relaxing the goal to minimize the expected monoculture error, we consider a simple sample-splitting strategy from Aden-Ali et al. (2024) in Appendix A . We observe that in the realizable proper learning case, a result from Aden-Ali et al. (2024) implies that splitting the sample S S of size 2 ​ n 2n into two independent halves and running an ERM on each yields a convergence rate of O ⁡ ( d / n ) O(d/n) , where d d is the VC dimension of the hypothesis class. This improves upon the standard expected error lower bound of Ω ⁡ ( d n ​ log ⁡ n d ) \Omega\left( rac{d}{n}\log rac{n}{d}ight) for a single ERM ( Haussler et al., 1994 ) , effectively “gaining” a logarithmic factor. It demonstrates a real separation between duplicating a single hypothesis trained on all the data and producing independent hypotheses by splitting the same data budget. This observation also highlights that if we do not require replicability and merely want low expected monoculture error for a given data budget, subsampling/splitting can be the right tool. For brevity, omitted proofs are relegated to Appendix C . 1.1 Related Work The phenomenon of algorithmic monoculture was formalized by Kleinberg and Raghavan (2021) , who demonstrated that while shared scoring rules may appear locally optimal for decision-makers, they introduce correlated failures that can reduce overall social welfare compared to noisy, independent evaluators. Bommasani et al. (2022) provided crucial empirical grounding for this theory, introducing the metric of outcome homogenization to quantify the extent to which distinct systems, specifically those relying on shared pre-trained components, systematically exclude the same individuals. This work supports the “component sharing hypothesis”, suggesting that the widespread adoption of the same foundation model or models trained on the same data by different agents exacerbates systemic exclusion. Complementing these findings, Black et al. (2022) and Marx et al. (2020) explore the "Rashomon Effect" or model multiplicity, highlighting that for many tasks, there exists a multiplicity of equally accurate models that nonetheless yield conflicting predictions for individual subjects. While multiplicity implies that diversity is theoretically achievable, standard training pipelines often fail to realize it without explicit intervention. Extending monoculture analysis to strategic settings, Peng and Garg (2024) examined two-sided matching markets, showing that while monoculture can help applicants identify viable matches, it disproportionately increases outcome variance for high-risk individuals. Unlike these works, which primarily characterize the existence and societal impact of correlated errors, our paper focuses on the learning-theoretic limits of overcoming them. Our work is also related to self-consistency Cooper et al. (2023) , which measures agreement between predicted labels across training samples without reference to the true label, while our goal is to control the label-dependent joint error of individually accurate predictors. We provide a detailed discussion and additional related work on self-consistency, model multiplicity, predictive multiplicity, algorithmic fairness, and replicability in Appendix B . 2 Model We focus on the binary classification task in the Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning setting. Monoculture Robust Learning Lee Cohen Affiliation: Stanford University Jon Kleinberg Affiliation: Cornell University Omer Reingold Affiliation: Stanford University Abstract We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture ( Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021 ) : the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output k k individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on k k independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness , and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all k k hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability ( Impagliazzo et al., 2022 ) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is ρ ho -replicable, then running it independently k k times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with k k , controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and ρ ho . We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to γ \gamma can require a sample-size multiplier of t = Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / γ ) ) t=\Omega(\log(1/\gamma)) . 1 Introduction In many real-world settings, people find themselves in situations where k k competing agents (or firms) offer the same type of opportunity or benefit, and each agent uses a learned decision rule to decide whether to extend an offer to a given individual. The individual may receive offers from multiple agents but ultimately accepts at most one. Examples include loan approvals across multiple banks, screening across multiple employers, ticket access for the same concert through different agencies, discounted travel offers during the holidays across competing platforms, or promotional discounts (e.g., a discounted haircut) across several salons in the same promotion network. If these agents rely on the same model, e.g., a single ad system that serves the ads for all the agents, their mistakes can become correlated, and the same individual can be rejected by all k k agents, even though the environment appears to provide multiple “chances.” This is the problem of algorithmic monoculture ( Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021 ) , in which the use of a common underlying model by multiple competing firms leads to correlated errors and consequently adverse consequences for individuals (and sometimes for the firms themselves). It is a common concern with modern machine learning systems, which are often deployed in settings where multiple providers use a common training pipeline and/or common dataset, and therefore their algorithms may repeatedly misclassify the same inputs . This means that even if an individual appears to be getting k k “tries” at an opportunity when they apply to k k different providers, they might in fact be getting something that more resembles a single try at the opportunity, since the misclassifications of all k k providers’ models are very similar. In this paper, we seek strategies to mitigate the negative effects of algorithmic monoculture, asking: if we only have access to one dataset, can we still produce k k accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is significantly lower than a single hypothesis? We formalize this question in the Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) setting by introducing individual monoculture robustness and its average analogue, expected monoculture robustness . We consider a learner that, given a single sample S ∼ 𝒟 n S\sim\mathcal{D}^{n} , outputs k k hypotheses h 1 , … , h k h_{1},\ldots,h_{k} , and measure monoculture failure via the conjunctive error : the event that all k k hypotheses misclassify a fixed point x x or, in expectation, a random point x ∼ 𝒟 X x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X} . This captures the “shared blind spot” that motivates monoculture concerns: beyond standard accuracy guarantees, it cares about the correlation of errors across the returned hypotheses, not just their marginal risks. This has a direct connection to algorithmic fairness ( Dwork et al., 2012 ) . Fairness and accuracy guarantees are typically stated for a single predictor, but in the settings above an individual effectively faces k k predictors in parallel (or over short time horizons), and what matters is the chance that all of them reject the individual. When errors are correlated across agents, “apply to more places” or “try another place” provides far less protection than one would expect under independence, and the harm can be concentrated on the same people or groups across many decision-makers. Monoculture robustness is designed to capture this concern by shifting attention from marginal error of each model to the joint failure probability across the k k models. A notable conceptual point is that monoculture failure can arise from two sources of randomness. Sometimes the error is sample-driven : for a point x x , most internal random seeds fail whenever the drawn sample is unrepresentative for x x . In this regime, rerunning the same algorithm on the same sample will not help much, and reducing the conjunctive error requires genuinely more data. Other times the error is internal randomness driven : for a typical sample S S , there are many seeds that predict the correct label, so rerunning with fresh randomness can reduce the probability that all k k runs land in the “bad” seeds. This separation guides our lower bound and the positive results. Throughout this work, we study both fundamental limits on monoculture robustness and concrete procedures for achieving it, including ERM-based and replicable learners. Contributions. Motivated by practical monoculture failures and the desire to “simulate” independence from a single dataset, we outline our contributions as follows. 1. Problem formulation. In section 2 , we formalize monoculture robustness for PAC learning by modeling a learner that, given a single dataset, outputs k k accurate hypotheses intended to serve k k agents. We quantify monoculture failure via conjunctive error and distinguish expected monoculture error from the stronger individual version. We also clarify when individual guarantees are meaningful, namely for a point x x with nontrivial single-run error of the base learning algorithm q x q_{x} (it is inherently uninformative to demand small joint failure when the single-run error is large). 2. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.24932 (cs) [Submitted on 18 Nov 2026] Title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems Authors: Priyanka Sinha , Sugam Pandey View a PDF of the paper titled Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems, by Priyanka Sinha and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable. Comments: Accepted at the Thirteenth Annual Conference on Advances in Cognitive Systems (ACS), Edinburgh, United Kingdom, October 6-9, 2026. items.content: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems Sugam Pandey Abstract When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer’s behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model’s self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541,621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2% correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2%); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5% of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable. priyanka.sinha.iitg@gmail.com sugam@docyt.com Docyt Inc., San Jose, CA 95110 USA ORCID (P. Sinha): https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7971-4449 1 Introduction A growing class of cognitive systems pairs a capable statistical model with a human who reviews its output. The model proposes; the human confirms or corrects; the corrections become the next round of training data. Medical-imaging triage, content moderation, and the AI-assisted bookkeeping system we study here all share this architecture. As the model improves, an awkward question surfaces: most of the human reviews now agree with the model. In the system we analyze, expert bookkeepers verify model-categorized financial transactions, and over a recent six-month window they confirmed the model’s prediction unchanged 71% of the time . The humans are expensive and finite. Which of them is the joint system still relying on, and for what? The instinctive answers are about activity : keep the reviewers who do the most work, who agree with their peers, who have been here longest, or who decide fastest and rarely change their minds. We will show that every one of these answers is wrong, and that they are wrong for the same reason. The property that actually governs a reviewer’s value to the joint system is not how much they do or how confidently they do it, but how well their confidence tracks their correctness, their metacognitive calibration ( Flavell, 1979 ; Fleming and Lau, 2014 ) . A reviewer who is fast and decisive and right is the most valuable agent in the system; a reviewer who is fast and decisive and wrong is the most dangerous, because the system, retrained on their confident corrections, inherits their error. Behaviorally, before we look at outcomes, the two are identical. This paper develops that observation into a trait theory of reviewer value, and tests it. We make three contributions to the study of human-AI cognitive systems. A Trait Theory (Section 3 ). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.24880 (cs) [Submitted on 18 Nov 2026] Title: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs Authors: Yuzhuo Li , Pasan Gunawardena , Yunwei Li View a PDF of the paper titled Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs, by Yuzhuo Li and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves. items.content: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs Yuzhuo Li Pasan Gunawardena and Yunwei Li † † thanks: Manuscript draft, November 2026. † † thanks: The authors are with the ELITEGrid Research Laboratory, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada (e-mail: yuzhuo@ualberta.ca; pasan@ualberta.ca; yunwei.li@ualberta.ca). Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization’s own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves. Index Terms: Agentic AI, large language models, power electronics, electromagnetic transients, local deployment, capability evaluation, energy consumption. I Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new possibilities for industrial application and academic innovation. However, the stochastic nature of its output limits its use in safety-critical applications. To overcome this limitation, agentic AI built on large language models (LLMs) has been developed. In an agent, the model calls tools, reads the returned results and determines the next action, so that computation and verification beyond its own ability are delegated to dedicated software. Moreover, feedback from a simulator in the loop has been shown to improve the task success rate substantially [ 1 ] . Such agents were first applied to software engineering [ 2 ] and have since spread to other engineering domains (Section II ). Power electronics, and the power systems it increasingly shapes, are a natural field of application. Although the field is built on physical hardware, simulation models have become accurate and efficient enough to support much of the design, verification and analysis work over the life cycle of a system. In addition, simulation results can be verified numerically. In power electronics, engineers solve design and study problems by iteration. As shown in Fig. 1 , a converter is modelled, simulated, measured against its specification and revised. A study of the network it connects to runs the same loop over faults, settings and operating points. Until recently, the loop was closed manually, i.e., an LLM used as an advisor remains outside it, and the engineer still runs the simulator, inspects the waveforms and makes the next modification. In contrast, an agent closes the loop itself [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Through a tool protocol such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), it builds or edits the simulation model, or submits simulation requests, reads the measured result and chooses the next action. An agent of this kind needs only a workstation that hosts the simulator and a model to drive it. Therefore, such an agent is within reach of laboratories and of the industrial groups that design drives, converters and protection. Fig. 1: The simulation workflow of power electronics and the systems it connects to, and where an agent enters it. A specification is met by building or modifying a simulation model, simulating it, measuring the result against the specification and revising until it is met or shown to be infeasible; the deliverable is a model, a setting or a report. Until recently the engineer closed this loop, with a language model at most advising from outside; an agent closes it itself. The agent’s model is served from a cloud API or from a device on the premises, and on a local device every run is paid for in four quantities: power, energy, tokens and time. Where the agent runs matters as much as what it can do. It can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises, and the choice between them is often determined by data-governance requirements before performance is considered. For organizations that handle sensitive designs, customer data or export-controlled material, or whose simulators are restricted to on-site use, local deployment is the natural choice (Section II ). Local deployment also makes the agent an electrical load on the organization’s own equipment. Every run consumes power and energy on a device the organization owns, generates tokens and occupies a simulator licence for hours. How much a task consumes depends on the choices of the deployment, and neither public leaderboards nor prices give the cost of completing a task. Therefore, four quantities have to be measured, each in its own unit: 1) the power drawn by the inference device, which determines the rating of its power supply; 2) the energy consumed until the task ends, which determines the electricity cost; 3) the number of tokens generated by the model, since the token budget is the only limit enforced by the agent software itself; and 4) the wall-clock time, during which the device, the simulator licence and the engineer awaiting the result are occupied. The questions that industrial groups ask of such agents are practical, e.g., what the agent can be trusted to do and what it costs to run. The published work reviewed in Section II answers the first of these for cloud-hosted models. However, what a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework for locally deployed engineering agents is presented in this paper. The main work is summarized as follows: 1) Starting from the structure of the agent loop, expressions for the power, energy, token count and time on an inference device are derived, together with an expression for the expected cost of a task that is run until it succeeds. 2) A unified procedure is built, which tests various agents on the same tasks under identical conditions, checks every result independently of the agent’s own report, and records the four quantities for every run. 3) The procedure is applied to tasks that range from the converter level to the system level in simulation environments, and the derived expressions are compared with the measurements. It should be noted that this study does not attempt an exhaustive evaluation of agents, and its counts are not a ranking of models. Instead, it is an exploration of what a local deployment involves. Its main contribution is not any single figure, but the considerations it identifies and a procedure for evaluating them objectively and fairly. Moreover, the capability of agentic AI is changing quickly. The models measured here will be superseded, and some of the boundaries reported will shift. Therefore, this paper is offered as a first template, i.e., an example that a group considering a local agent can repeat on its own tasks, devices and models. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II gives the background of local deployment and reviews the related work. Section III analyses the constraints and the mechanism of local deployment, and derives the four quantities on the inference device. Section IV introduces the measurement framework. The measured capability and costs are presented in Section V and discussed in Section VI . Finally, Section VII concludes this paper. II Background and Related Work TABLE I: Prior Work Related to This Paper: What Is Placed in the Loop and What Is Measured Category of work Simulator in loop Open weights Energy measured Local vs. cloud Agents for converter design [ 3 , 4 , 1 , 5 , 7 , 6 ] yes no no no Agents for other engineering tools and power system solvers [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] yes some no capability only Energy of agents on generic benchmarks [ 16 , 2 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] no yes yes by estimate [ 20 , 21 ] Capability indices, open-weight vs. closed [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] no yes no implied This paper yes yes yes, per run yes, same loop II-A Industrial Context and Motivation Agentic AI is attracting wide attention and adoption. For example, Gartner [ 25 ] expects agentic AI to make at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions autonomously by 2028, up from none in 2024, and to be built into a third of enterprise software by then. However, Gartner also expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by 2027 due to escalating cost, unclear value or inadequate risk control. For an engineering agent, the choice between a cloud API and an inference device on the premises is often determined by data-governance requirements before performance is considered. Organizations that handle sensitive designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot send their files to a vendor, and an agent reads and writes the engineering files themselves. In line with this, interviews across engineering firms find adoption limited by security and regulatory requirements and legacy toolchains rather than by model capability [ 26 ] . The simulation software is a second consideration. Simulators are licensed on premises. Some installations can be reached remotely, while others are restricted to on-site use. Where the connection policy of an organization is strict, the model has to be deployed locally. For such organizations, local deployment is the natural choice, and the demand is likely to grow. Two observations support this. In a 2026 survey of 1,000 senior executives, 68% said that meeting data residency and sovereignty requirements across geographies is challenging [ 27 ] . Moreover, the interest in small open-weight models is driven in part by the prospect of running agents on hardware an organization controls [ 2 ] . Local deployment of such an agent is a multidisciplinary undertaking. The power electronics, the data, the algorithms and the simulation tasks are deeply coupled, and the deployment has to bring all of them together. A local run that operates for forty minutes at constant power and fails has consumed energy and time that are not recorded in any bill. How much a task consumes depends on the choices that follow once the agent is local, i.e., which model and quantization [ 19 , 2 ] , what output-token budget and how much reasoning effort [ 16 ] , whether measured results are fed back to the agent [ 1 ] , how many inference nodes, and which tasks to keep local. Each choice is made under two uncertainties, i.e., where the capability of a local agent on the organization’s own tasks ends, and what each option costs. For the first, public leaderboards [ 22 , 23 ] do not say whether a model can edit a Simulink model, read a waveform correctly or keep a protected requirement intact. For the second, neither the price per token nor the price of the hardware gives the cost of completing a task, because a failed run has to be repeated and its cost is added to that of the successful one [ 17 , 18 ] . The questions that industrial groups ask of such agents are practical: 1) what can the agent be trusted to do, and on what evidence; 2) what does it cost to run; 3) what data leaves the site when a cloud model is used; and 4) which simulation-heavy workflows would benefit. II-B Related Work Prior work relevant to these questions falls into four categories. What each category places in the loop and what it measures are summarized in Table I . The first category builds agents for converter design. Coupling a language model to physics-informed surrogates [ 3 , 28 , 4 ] , to SPICE [ 1 , 6 ] or to a complete design flow [ 5 , 7 ] improves the task success rate substantially, e.g., from 14% to 46% and from 25% to 85% on 269 switched-mode supply tasks in one study [ 1 ] . However, all of these run on closed models, and none measures power or energy. A recent tutorial [ 29 ] lists cost, energy, latency and robustness among the considerations that prototype-stage AI for power electronics has under-emphasized. It also observes that practitioners have not yet seen the real boundaries of the methods. Moreover, the one Simulink benchmark that includes open-weight models and power-electronic tasks reports scores for a single task family and does not say where the models ran [ 30 ] . The second category applies agents to other engineering tools: chemistry laboratories [ 8 , 31 ] , circuit design [ 32 , 33 ] , CAE tools [ 9 , 10 , 34 , 11 ] and power system solvers [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 35 ] . III-A Differences Between Cloud and Local Deployment A local run and a cloud run differ by design only in where the model executes (Section IV-A ), and that location determines what can be measured. For a closed model served through an API, they can only be estimated, with an uncertainty that a local measurement does not carry. In the cloud, the operator chooses a model and a reasoning tier and pays per token, while capacity, context length and generation rate are handled by the provider.
