items.raw_text: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs Yuzhuo Li Pasan Gunawardena and Yunwei Li † † thanks: Manuscript draft, November 2026. † † thanks: The authors are with the ELITEGrid Research Laboratory, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada (e-mail: yuzhuo@ualberta.ca; pasan@ualberta.ca; yunwei.li@ualberta.ca). Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization’s own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves. Index Terms: Agentic AI, large language models, power electronics, electromagnetic transients, local deployment, capability evaluation, energy consumption. I Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new possibilities for industrial application and academic innovation. However, the stochastic nature of its output limits its use in safety-critical applications. To overcome this limitation, agentic AI built on large language models (LLMs) has been developed. In an agent, the model calls tools, reads the returned results and determines the next action, so that computation and verification beyond its own ability are delegated to dedicated software. Moreover, feedback from a simulator in the loop has been shown to improve the task success rate substantially [ 1 ] . Such agents were first applied to software engineering [ 2 ] and have since spread to other engineering domains (Section II ). Power electronics, and the power systems it increasingly shapes, are a natural field of application. Although the field is built on physical hardware, simulation models have become accurate and efficient enough to support much of the design, verification and analysis work over the life cycle of a system. In addition, simulation results can be verified numerically. In power electronics, engineers solve design and study problems by iteration. As shown in Fig. 1 , a converter is modelled, simulated, measured against its specification and revised. A study of the network it connects to runs the same loop over faults, settings and operating points. Until recently, the loop was closed manually, i.e., an LLM used as an advisor remains outside it, and the engineer still runs the simulator, inspects the waveforms and makes the next modification. In contrast, an agent closes the loop itself [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Through a tool protocol such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), it builds or edits the simulation model, or submits simulation requests, reads the measured result and chooses the next action. An agent of this kind needs only a workstation that hosts the simulator and a model to drive it. Therefore, such an agent is within reach of laboratories and of the industrial groups that design drives, converters and protection. Fig. 1: The simulation workflow of power electronics and the systems it connects to, and where an agent enters it. A specification is met by building or modifying a simulation model, simulating it, measuring the result against the specification and revising until it is met or shown to be infeasible; the deliverable is a model, a setting or a report. Until recently the engineer closed this loop, with a language model at most advising from outside; an agent closes it itself. The agent’s model is served from a cloud API or from a device on the premises, and on a local device every run is paid for in four quantities: power, energy, tokens and time. Where the agent runs matters as much as what it can do. It can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises, and the choice between them is often determined by data-governance requirements before performance is considered. For organizations that handle sensitive designs, customer data or export-controlled material, or whose simulators are restricted to on-site use, local deployment is the natural choice (Section II ). Local deployment also makes the agent an electrical load on the organization’s own equipment. Every run consumes power and energy on a device the organization owns, generates tokens and occupies a simulator licence for hours. How much a task consumes depends on the choices of the deployment, and neither public leaderboards nor prices give the cost of completing a task. Therefore, four quantities have to be measured, each in its own unit: 1) the power drawn by the inference device, which determines the rating of its power supply; 2) the energy consumed until the task ends, which determines the electricity cost; 3) the number of tokens generated by the model, since the token budget is the only limit enforced by the agent software itself; and 4) the wall-clock time, during which the device, the simulator licence and the engineer awaiting the result are occupied. The questions that industrial groups ask of such agents are practical, e.g., what the agent can be trusted to do and what it costs to run. The published work reviewed in Section II answers the first of these for cloud-hosted models. However, what a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework for locally deployed engineering agents is presented in this paper. The main work is summarized as follows: 1) Starting from the structure of the agent loop, expressions for the power, energy, token count and time on an inference device are derived, together with an expression for the expected cost of a task that is run until it succeeds. 2) A unified procedure is built, which tests various agents on the same tasks under identical conditions, checks every result independently of the agent’s own report, and records the four quantities for every run. 3) The procedure is applied to tasks that range from the converter level to the system level in simulation environments, and the derived expressions are compared with the measurements. It should be noted that this study does not attempt an exhaustive evaluation of agents, and its counts are not a ranking of models. Instead, it is an exploration of what a local deployment involves. Its main contribution is not any single figure, but the considerations it identifies and a procedure for evaluating them objectively and fairly. Moreover, the capability of agentic AI is changing quickly. The models measured here will be superseded, and some of the boundaries reported will shift. Therefore, this paper is offered as a first template, i.e., an example that a group considering a local agent can repeat on its own tasks, devices and models. Section III analyses the constraints and the mechanism of local deployment, and derives the four quantities on the inference device. Section IV introduces the measurement framework. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.24869 (cs) [Submitted on 18 Nov 2026] Title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules Authors: Mingliang Zhai , Chuanhao Li , Jiaming Tan , Zhen Li , Yuwei Wu , Yunde Jia , Zian Meng , Yuanyang Yin , Kaipeng Zhang View a PDF of the paper titled WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules, by Mingliang Zhai and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes. items.content: \github https://alaya-lab.github.io/WorldRuler \Code https://github.com/AlayaLab/WorldRuler \Data https://huggingface.co/datasets/AlayaLab/RuleVerse \contact chuanhao.li@shanda.com, wuyuwei@bit.edu.cn WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules Mingliang Zhai* Affiliation: Alaya Lab Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Technology Chuanhao Li † \dagger , ‡ \ddagger Affiliation: Alaya Lab Jiaming Tan Affiliation: Alaya Lab Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Technology Zhen Li Affiliation: Alaya Lab Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute Yuwei Wu † \dagger Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Technology Yunde Jia Affiliation: The University of Tokyo Zian Meng Affiliation: Shenzhen MSU-BIT University Yuanyang Yin Affiliation: Shenzhen MSU-BIT University Kaipeng Zhang Affiliation: Alaya Lab Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute Abstract Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization . The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes. † † date: November 18, 2026 † † footnotetext: * Work done during internship at Alaya Lab, † \dagger Corresponding author, ‡ \ddagger Project lead Figure 1 : WorldRuler enables persistent, rule-governed generative worlds. The saved rules and world state allow the player to collect the key and open the door after loading, demonstrating Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization . 1 Introduction Rules govern the consequences of player actions, creating different gameplay goals and strategies even within similar scenes and action spaces Hunicke et al. (2004) . For example, Cat Mario subverts conventional game rules, where seemingly safe platforms collapse and power-ups can kill players, while It Takes Two introduces unique interaction rules, such as using nails to create paths across otherwise impassable gaps. These examples motivate generative game worlds He et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2026a) that consistently follow user-defined rules beyond conventional real-world behaviors. Achieving this goal requires connecting user-defined interaction logic with world-state maintenance and visual generation. Code World Model Chen et al. (2026b) and Programmable World Model Huang et al. (2026) maintain executable world states and translate them into video generation conditions. Supporting persistent interaction requires both Rule-State Persistence across saving and loading and Rule-to-Visual Realization on designated visual instances. Rule-State Persistence requires jointly preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading. As shown in Figure 1 , consider a rule chain in which a sword attack defeats a monster, the monster drops a key, and the key unlocks a door. If the player saves before collecting the key, restoration must preserve the defeated monster, dropped key, closed door, and remaining rules. A restorable world must therefore retain the states and rule dependencies that govern future interactions, including information absent from the current view. Rule-to-Visual Realization requires grounding rule-specified objects and attributes in visual instances to realize changes at the correct time. This is particularly important when the affected object is initially unseen Duan et al. (2026) ; Gu et al. (2026) . For example, if a switch opens a gate outside the current view, the gate should already be open when the player first sees it. The stored state must constrain this first appearance and remain effective in subsequent interactions. Graph representations provide structured conditions for object relations and interactions in video generation Shah et al. (2026) ; Park et al. (2026) . Custom rules further require persistent object binding and attribute control that supports compatible appearance and motion changes without disrupting unrelated content Li et al. (2025) ; Chu et al. (2025) . In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback through an executable 3D rule graph. The graph organizes rule definitions, dependencies, object identities, and attribute states together with spatial information. Rules and world states are saved and restored jointly, allowing subsequent actions to be evaluated against the restored conditions. Dynamic object binding associates rule-specified entities with visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. Perceptual feedback verifies generated outcomes and updates object correspondences and local geometry for subsequent binding and generation, while keeping rule-prescribed states separate from visual evidence. To enforce these rule-prescribed states, we introduce an object attribute state replacement mechanism that reads object attribute states during denoising and replaces them according to the prescribed targets, correcting deviations in the controlled attributes. We complement this mechanism with counterfactual reconstruction training to produce coherent visual outcomes. Counterfactual reconstruction learns the visual realization of each state, while paired supervision encourages compatible changes and preservation of unrelated content. Training constrains these visual adjustments to remain compatible with the prescribed states, supporting the required appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with other objects and attributes. To support counterfactual reconstruction training and rule consistency evaluation, we develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat Puig et al. (2024) , resulting in RuleVerse , a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed annotations of object states, trigger conditions, rule consequences, and event timing. RuleVerse covers diverse triggers and state changes, multi-step rule dependencies, and rules that take effect before the affected objects become visible. RuleVerse supports the evaluation of rule-state consistency across saving and loading, the accurate realization of prescribed outcomes on designated objects and attributes, and preservation of unrelated content. Experiments on the public WorldState-Bench Ki et al. (2026) and our RuleVerse demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler. In summary, our contributions are threefold: • We propose WorldRuler, an executable 3D rule graph framework with dynamic object binding and perceptual feedback for rule persistence and visual realization. • We introduce object attribute state replacement with counterfactual reconstruction training to realize prescribed changes while preserving unrelated content. • We construct RuleVerse through automated data collection and annotation in GTA-V and Habitat, supporting counterfactual training and rule consistency evaluation. 2 Related Work 2.1 Video World Models Video world models predict observations from visual history and actions for exploration Kim et al. (2020) ; Yang et al. (2024) . Early methods learn environment dynamics and action-conditioned generation Bruce et al. (2024) ; Alonso et al. (2024) ; Valevski et al. (2025) . Recent work advances real-time control and long-horizon consistency. Yume1.5 Mao et al. (2026) combines context compression and attention distillation for real-time generation with text-controlled events. Long interactions, however, introduce inconsistencies when revisiting scenes. WorldPlay Sun et al. (2025) improves geometric consistency through reconstituted context memory. Matrix-Game 3.0 Wang et al. (2026) combines camera-aware memory retrieval and self-correction training. AlayaWorld Team et al. (2026) uses a streaming 3D point cache for spatiotemporal consistency. AlayaVista Tan et al. (2026) uses panoramic latent states and viewport rendering for perspective generation. Alaya-EVOKE Yin et al. (2026) combines external spatial memory with long-horizon supervision. Despite these advances, persistent adherence to user-defined rules remains insufficiently addressed. WorldRuler maintains rule states to constrain subsequent video generation. 2.2 Controllable Video Generation Controllable video generation aims to realize specified changes while preserving unrelated content. Early methods use camera poses and motion trajectories for generation control Wang et al. (2024) ; He et al. (2024) ; Yin et al. (2023) . H3-World Chen et al. (2026a) translates language instructions into aligned character and camera controls. More complex object and structural changes require explicit representations. WorldCraft Gu et al. (2026) uses 3D representations and world-coordinate constraints for object manipulation. CustomX Wang et al. (2025) customizes characters, actions, and scenes using 3D assets. SolarRenderer Fang et al. (2026) adapts pretrained video generators to structured scene representations. GraphVid Shah et al. (2026) uses interaction graphs for multi-entity control. Park et al. Park et al. (2026) introduce graph-aligned denoising supervision through paired video-graph modifications. However, these methods do not explicitly maintain rule-dependent states across interactions. WorldRuler binds executable rule states to persistent visual instances and uses attribute replacement to realize prescribed changes on designated objects while preserving unrelated visual content. 2.3 State and Rules in World Models Persistent states maintain interaction consequences beyond current observations. Early world models learn latent dynamics Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) ; Hafner et al. (2025) , and structured representations capture object identities and spatial relationships Wu et al. (2023) . However, unobserved states cannot always be recovered from visual history. LiveWorld Duan et al. (2026) models dynamic objects outside the current view. Executable logic enables explicit control over state transitions. Code World Model Chen et al. (2026b) uses a coding agent to maintain world states and compile them into proxy videos. Programmable World Model Huang et al. (2026) maintains global states through executable programs and converts them into spatial generation conditions. State World Models Ki et al. (2026) execute interaction rules and updates states using generated observations. Building on explicit state maintenance and rule execution, WorldRuler jointly restores rule definitions, dependencies, and execution states, ensuring their consequences are realized on designated visual instances. 3 WorldRuler 3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview Given an initial visual observation I 0 I_{0} , user-defined rules ℛ \mathcal{R} , and a sequence of player actions, WorldRuler generates interactive videos that follow these rules. An executable 3D rule graph 𝒢 t \mathcal{G}_{t} maintains rule definitions and dependencies, an execution state X t X_{t} records object attributes and rule progress, and bindings ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} associate rule entities with 3D objects and visual instances. Together, these representations determine subsequent interactions and persist when objects leave the view or a session is saved. As shown in Fig. 2 , generation proceeds in consecutive windows. For window n n , the executor evaluates actions U n U_{n} against the current state and produces a sequence of object states 𝒮 n \mathcal{S}_{n} . These states and their spatial bindings form generation conditions C n C_{n} V ^ n \displaystyle\widehat{V}_{n} ∼ p θ , ϕ ​ ( V n ∣ I 0 , H n , U n , C n ) , \displaystyle\sim p_{\theta,\phi}\!\left(V_{n}\mid I_{0},H_{n},U_{n},C_{n}\right), (1) C n \displaystyle C_{n} = Condition ⁡ ( 𝒢 n , ℬ n , 𝒮 n ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{Condition}\!\left(\mathcal{G}_{n},\mathcal{B}_{n},\mathcal{S}_{n}\right), where H n H_{n} denotes previously generated visual context, θ \theta denotes the video generator parameters, and ϕ \phi denotes trainable attribute replacement parameters. The state sequence follows from actions and rule execution within the current window, without future outcomes from reference videos. Object binding identifies where rule targets apply, attribute replacement corrects those regions during denoising, and perception updates correspondences and event evidence for subsequent windows. The graph and its joint checkpoint support Rule-State Persistence, while binding and replacement support Rule-to-Visual Realization. Figure 2 : Overview of WorldRuler. Rule execution updates persistent object states, dynamic binding associates rule entities with 3D instances and their current image regions, and local attribute replacement corrects denoising estimates for the next sampling update. Rules, states, execution progress, and bindings are saved and restored jointly. Independent perceptual feedback informs subsequent windows. Scene and point cloud images come from the demo visualization, while the remaining flows and gate-state comparison illustrate the mechanism. 3.2 Executable 3D Rule Graph and Persistence The rule graph organizes object identities, spatial information, and interaction logic in a shared representation. Object nodes carry persistent identities, semantic descriptions, 3D support, and attribute states. Rule nodes specify triggers, state preconditions, and effect assignments. Typed edges distinguish action subjects, action targets, precondition objects, and effect targets, allowing a consequence to occur away from its trigger. Shared attributes and event conditions express dependencies between rules. For example, collecting a key changes the possession state required by an unlocking rule. Initial objects and spatial information are established from the initial observation and available scene geometry. References to objects that cannot yet be localized remain in the graph for later binding. Let S t S_{t} collect object attributes and let q t q_{t} contain event history, rule activation records, transition progress, and pending effects. The execution state is X t = ( S t , q t ) X_{t}=(S_{t},q_{t}) and evolves according to X t + 1 = Execute ℛ ⁡ ( X t , u t , e t ) , X_{t+1}=\operatorname{Execute}_{\mathcal{R}}\!\left(X_{t},u_{t},e_{t}\right), (2) where u t u_{t} is the current action and e t e_{t} is accepted event evidence. The executor evaluates action, state, spatial, and event-order conditions before assigning effects to their designated objects. Rules requiring action completion consume confirmed completion events, so an action request alone does not satisfy them. Unknown attributes remain explicitly unknown and cannot satisfy a precondition through negation. For changes with a duration, the state records current values, targets, and transition progress. Generation receives the effective value at each time, while dependent predicates respect transition completion. This prevents a partially opening door from prematurely satisfying an open-door condition. Effects on invisible objects persist in the state. When an effect target is unresolved, the system retains its description, rule provenance, and event time until the target can be bound. A checkpoint jointly serializes the graph, execution state, and bindings 𝒞 t \displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{t} = Save ⁡ ( 𝒢 t , X t , ℬ t ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{Save}\!\left(\mathcal{G}_{t},X_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t}\right), (3) Load ⁡ ( 𝒞 t ) \displaystyle\operatorname{Load}(\mathcal{C}_{t}) = ( 𝒢 t , X t , ℬ t ) . \displaystyle=\left(\mathcal{G}_{t},X_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t}\right). The checkpoint path in Fig. 2 restores rule definitions, object identities, and execution progress so that subsequent actions continue from the saved conditions. For example, a checkpoint taken after defeating a monster but before collecting its key retains the defeated monster, the key on the ground, the closed door, and the remaining collection and unlocking rules. Continuing generation additionally requires visual boundary context corresponding to the restored state. Images may vary with sampling, while identical subsequent actions and event evidence should produce consistent rule decisions. 3.3 Dynamic Object Binding and Perceptual Feedback Dynamic object binding first identifies which scene instance a rule addresses and then determines where that instance can be controlled in the current view. Semantic, appearance, and spatial consistency associate candidate instances with rule entities, and ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} stores these correspondences. Objects of the same category retain distinct identities, while viewpoint changes, occlusion, and reappearance preserve established bindings. For localized objects, camera projection and instance segmentation Ravi et al. (2024) provide spatiotemporal masks M i M_{i} , restricted by visibility and occlusion. Rules can update an object’s persistent state while it is invisible. Given an established 3D binding, the stored state is assigned to the projected region before generating the window in which the object first appears. A gate opened outside the view is therefore conditioned as open from its first appearance, without repeating the opening action. Effects on entirely unlocalized entities remain pending until reliable correspondences become available. First-appearance control thus depends on spatial grounding established before generation. The executed scene geometry guides layout, camera motion, and object motion, while effective states and changes form global and object-level visual descriptions. Each local condition specifies an identity, spatiotemporal support, and structured attribute targets. Surface changes use object surface support, while motion and deformation cover the current geometry and rule-executed trajectory, excluding foreground occluders and unrelated instances. Unknown attributes are omitted from local control, and completed changes persist as resulting-state conditions. Perception independently estimates identity, visibility, visual attributes, and action completion from generated frames, without receiving desired rule outcomes as answer cues. Evidence passing identity, confidence, and temporal validity checks updates bindings, local geometry, and ordinary observable state, and supplies events for subsequent rules that require visual confirmation. Rule-prescribed states and observed outcomes are recorded separately. If a gate appears closed despite an open-state requirement, the prescribed state is retained, and the observed discrepancy guides correction in subsequent generation windows. Feedback affects only windows generated after its acceptance, without rewriting delivered video or treating unconfirmed outcomes as successful. 3.4 Object Attribute State Replacement Object binding determines the support of an edit, and attribute state replacement adjusts its visual representation to the rule target. Figure 3 (a) expands the Replace module in the overview into local attribute reading, target correction, and insertion into the sampling update. Reading Local Attributes. Let z σ z_{\sigma} denote the video latent at noise level σ > 0 \sigma>0 and let v θ v_{\theta} be the predicted velocity. Under the generator’s parameterization, the clean estimate is z ^ 0 = z σ + σ ​ v θ ​ ( z σ , σ , C n ) . \widehat{z}_{0}=z_{\sigma}+\sigma v_{\theta}(z_{\sigma},\sigma,C_{n}). items.raw_text: \github https://alaya-lab.github.io/WorldRuler \Code https://github.com/AlayaLab/WorldRuler \Data https://huggingface.co/datasets/AlayaLab/RuleVerse \contact chuanhao.li@shanda.com, wuyuwei@bit.edu.cn WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules Mingliang Zhai* Affiliation: Alaya Lab Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Technology Chuanhao Li † \dagger , ‡ \ddagger Affiliation: Alaya Lab Jiaming Tan Affiliation: Alaya Lab Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Technology Zhen Li Affiliation: Alaya Lab Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute Yuwei Wu † \dagger Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Technology Yunde Jia Affiliation: The University of Tokyo Zian Meng Affiliation: Shenzhen MSU-BIT University Yuanyang Yin Affiliation: Shenzhen MSU-BIT University Kaipeng Zhang Affiliation: Alaya Lab Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute Abstract Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization . The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes. † † date: November 18, 2026 † † footnotetext: * Work done during internship at Alaya Lab, † \dagger Corresponding author, ‡ \ddagger Project lead Figure 1 : WorldRuler enables persistent, rule-governed generative worlds. The saved rules and world state allow the player to collect the key and open the door after loading, demonstrating Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization . 1 Introduction Rules govern the consequences of player actions, creating different gameplay goals and strategies even within similar scenes and action spaces Hunicke et al. (2004) . For example, Cat Mario subverts conventional game rules, where seemingly safe platforms collapse and power-ups can kill players, while It Takes Two introduces unique interaction rules, such as using nails to create paths across otherwise impassable gaps. These examples motivate generative game worlds He et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2026a) that consistently follow user-defined rules beyond conventional real-world behaviors. Achieving this goal requires connecting user-defined interaction logic with world-state maintenance and visual generation. Code World Model Chen et al. (2026b) and Programmable World Model Huang et al. (2026) maintain executable world states and translate them into video generation conditions. Supporting persistent interaction requires both Rule-State Persistence across saving and loading and Rule-to-Visual Realization on designated visual instances. Rule-State Persistence requires jointly preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading. As shown in Figure 1 , consider a rule chain in which a sword attack defeats a monster, the monster drops a key, and the key unlocks a door. If the player saves before collecting the key, restoration must preserve the defeated monster, dropped key, closed door, and remaining rules. A restorable world must therefore retain the states and rule dependencies that govern future interactions, including information absent from the current view. Rule-to-Visual Realization requires grounding rule-specified objects and attributes in visual instances to realize changes at the correct time. This is particularly important when the affected object is initially unseen Duan et al. (2026) ; Gu et al. (2026) . For example, if a switch opens a gate outside the current view, the gate should already be open when the player first sees it. The stored state must constrain this first appearance and remain effective in subsequent interactions. Graph representations provide structured conditions for object relations and interactions in video generation Shah et al. (2026) ; Park et al. (2026) . Custom rules further require persistent object binding and attribute control that supports compatible appearance and motion changes without disrupting unrelated content Li et al. (2025) ; Chu et al. (2025) . In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback through an executable 3D rule graph. The graph organizes rule definitions, dependencies, object identities, and attribute states together with spatial information. Rules and world states are saved and restored jointly, allowing subsequent actions to be evaluated against the restored conditions. Dynamic object binding associates rule-specified entities with visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. Perceptual feedback verifies generated outcomes and updates object correspondences and local geometry for subsequent binding and generation, while keeping rule-prescribed states separate from visual evidence. To enforce these rule-prescribed states, we introduce an object attribute state replacement mechanism that reads object attribute states during denoising and replaces them according to the prescribed targets, correcting deviations in the controlled attributes. We complement this mechanism with counterfactual reconstruction training to produce coherent visual outcomes. Counterfactual reconstruction learns the visual realization of each state, while paired supervision encourages compatible changes and preservation of unrelated content. Training constrains these visual adjustments to remain compatible with the prescribed states, supporting the required appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with other objects and attributes. To support counterfactual reconstruction training and rule consistency evaluation, we develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat Puig et al. (2024) , resulting in RuleVerse , a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed annotations of object states, trigger conditions, rule consequences, and event timing. RuleVerse covers diverse triggers and state changes, multi-step rule dependencies, and rules that take effect before the affected objects become visible. RuleVerse supports the evaluation of rule-state consistency across saving and loading, the accurate realization of prescribed outcomes on designated objects and attributes, and preservation of unrelated content. Experiments on the public WorldState-Bench Ki et al. (2026) and our RuleVerse demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler. In summary, our contributions are threefold: • We propose WorldRuler, an executable 3D rule graph framework with dynamic object binding and perceptual feedback for rule persistence and visual realization. • We introduce object attribute state replacement with counterfactual reconstruction training to realize prescribed changes while preserving unrelated content. • We construct RuleVerse through automated data collection and annotation in GTA-V and Habitat, supporting counterfactual training and rule consistency evaluation. 2 Related Work 2.1 Video World Models Video world models predict observations from visual history and actions for exploration Kim et al. (2020) ; Yang et al. (2024) . Early methods learn environment dynamics and action-conditioned generation Bruce et al. (2024) ; Alonso et al. (2024) ; Valevski et al. (2025) . Recent work advances real-time control and long-horizon consistency. Yume1.5 Mao et al. (2026) combines context compression and attention distillation for real-time generation with text-controlled events. Long interactions, however, introduce inconsistencies when revisiting scenes. WorldPlay Sun et al. (2025) improves geometric consistency through reconstituted context memory. Matrix-Game 3.0 Wang et al. (2026) combines camera-aware memory retrieval and self-correction training. AlayaWorld Team et al. (2026) uses a streaming 3D point cache for spatiotemporal consistency. AlayaVista Tan et al. (2026) uses panoramic latent states and viewport rendering for perspective generation. Alaya-EVOKE Yin et al. (2026) combines external spatial memory with long-horizon supervision. Despite these advances, persistent adherence to user-defined rules remains insufficiently addressed. WorldRuler maintains rule states to constrain subsequent video generation. 2.2 Controllable Video Generation Controllable video generation aims to realize specified changes while preserving unrelated content. Early methods use camera poses and motion trajectories for generation control Wang et al. (2024) ; He et al. (2024) ; Yin et al. (2023) . H3-World Chen et al. (2026a) translates language instructions into aligned character and camera controls. More complex object and structural changes require explicit representations. WorldCraft Gu et al. (2026) uses 3D representations and world-coordinate constraints for object manipulation. CustomX Wang et al. (2025) customizes characters, actions, and scenes using 3D assets. SolarRenderer Fang et al. (2026) adapts pretrained video generators to structured scene representations. GraphVid Shah et al. (2026) uses interaction graphs for multi-entity control. Park et al. Park et al. (2026) introduce graph-aligned denoising supervision through paired video-graph modifications. However, these methods do not explicitly maintain rule-dependent states across interactions. WorldRuler binds executable rule states to persistent visual instances and uses attribute replacement to realize prescribed changes on designated objects while preserving unrelated visual content. 2.3 State and Rules in World Models Persistent states maintain interaction consequences beyond current observations. Early world models learn latent dynamics Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) ; Hafner et al. (2025) , and structured representations capture object identities and spatial relationships Wu et al. (2023) . However, unobserved states cannot always be recovered from visual history. LiveWorld Duan et al. (2026) models dynamic objects outside the current view. Executable logic enables explicit control over state transitions. Code World Model Chen et al. (2026b) uses a coding agent to maintain world states and compile them into proxy videos. Programmable World Model Huang et al. (2026) maintains global states through executable programs and converts them into spatial generation conditions. State World Models Ki et al. (2026) execute interaction rules and updates states using generated observations. Building on explicit state maintenance and rule execution, WorldRuler jointly restores rule definitions, dependencies, and execution states, ensuring their consequences are realized on designated visual instances. 3 WorldRuler 3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview Given an initial visual observation I 0 I_{0} , user-defined rules ℛ \mathcal{R} , and a sequence of player actions, WorldRuler generates interactive videos that follow these rules. An executable 3D rule graph 𝒢 t \mathcal{G}_{t} maintains rule definitions and dependencies, an execution state X t X_{t} records object attributes and rule progress, and bindings ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} associate rule entities with 3D objects and visual instances. Together, these representations determine subsequent interactions and persist when objects leave the view or a session is saved. As shown in Fig. 2 , generation proceeds in consecutive windows. For window n n , the executor evaluates actions U n U_{n} against the current state and produces a sequence of object states 𝒮 n \mathcal{S}_{n} . These states and their spatial bindings form generation conditions C n C_{n} V ^ n \displaystyle\widehat{V}_{n} ∼ p θ , ϕ ​ ( V n ∣ I 0 , H n , U n , C n ) , \displaystyle\sim p_{\theta,\phi}\!\left(V_{n}\mid I_{0},H_{n},U_{n},C_{n}\right), (1) C n \displaystyle C_{n} = Condition ⁡ ( 𝒢 n , ℬ n , 𝒮 n ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{Condition}\!\left(\mathcal{G}_{n},\mathcal{B}_{n},\mathcal{S}_{n}\right), where H n H_{n} denotes previously generated visual context, θ \theta denotes the video generator parameters, and ϕ \phi denotes trainable attribute replacement parameters. The state sequence follows from actions and rule execution within the current window, without future outcomes from reference videos. Object binding identifies where rule targets apply, attribute replacement corrects those regions during denoising, and perception updates correspondences and event evidence for subsequent windows. The graph and its joint checkpoint support Rule-State Persistence, while binding and replacement support Rule-to-Visual Realization. Figure 2 : Overview of WorldRuler. Rule execution updates persistent object states, dynamic binding associates rule entities with 3D instances and their current image regions, and local attribute replacement corrects denoising estimates for the next sampling update. Rules, states, execution progress, and bindings are saved and restored jointly. Independent perceptual feedback informs subsequent windows. Scene and point cloud images come from the demo visualization, while the remaining flows and gate-state comparison illustrate the mechanism. 3.2 Executable 3D Rule Graph and Persistence The rule graph organizes object identities, spatial information, and interaction logic in a shared representation. Object nodes carry persistent identities, semantic descriptions, 3D support, and attribute states. Rule nodes specify triggers, state preconditions, and effect assignments. Typed edges distinguish action subjects, action targets, precondition objects, and effect targets, allowing a consequence to occur away from its trigger. Shared attributes and event conditions express dependencies between rules. For example, collecting a key changes the possession state required by an unlocking rule. Initial objects and spatial information are established from the initial observation and available scene geometry. References to objects that cannot yet be localized remain in the graph for later binding. Let S t S_{t} collect object attributes and let q t q_{t} contain event history, rule activation records, transition progress, and pending effects. The execution state is X t = ( S t , q t ) X_{t}=(S_{t},q_{t}) and evolves according to X t + 1 = Execute ℛ ⁡ ( X t , u t , e t ) , X_{t+1}=\operatorname{Execute}_{\mathcal{R}}\!\left(X_{t},u_{t},e_{t}\right), (2) where u t u_{t} is the current action and e t e_{t} is accepted event evidence. The executor evaluates action, state, spatial, and event-order conditions before assigning effects to their designated objects. Rules requiring action completion consume confirmed completion events, so an action request alone does not satisfy them. Unknown attributes remain explicitly unknown and cannot satisfy a precondition through negation. For changes with a duration, the state records current values, targets, and transition progress. Generation receives the effective value at each time, while dependent predicates respect transition completion. This prevents a partially opening door from prematurely satisfying an open-door condition. Effects on invisible objects persist in the state. When an effect target is unresolved, the system retains its description, rule provenance, and event time until the target can be bound. A checkpoint jointly serializes the graph, execution state, and bindings 𝒞 t \displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{t} = Save ⁡ ( 𝒢 t , X t , ℬ t ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{Save}\!\left(\mathcal{G}_{t},X_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t}\right), (3) Load ⁡ ( 𝒞 t ) \displaystyle\operatorname{Load}(\mathcal{C}_{t}) = ( 𝒢 t , X t , ℬ t ) . \displaystyle=\left(\mathcal{G}_{t},X_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t}\right). The checkpoint path in Fig. 2 restores rule definitions, object identities, and execution progress so that subsequent actions continue from the saved conditions. For example, a checkpoint taken after defeating a monster but before collecting its key retains the defeated monster, the key on the ground, the closed door, and the remaining collection and unlocking rules. Continuing generation additionally requires visual boundary context corresponding to the restored state. Images may vary with sampling, while identical subsequent actions and event evidence should produce consistent rule decisions. 3.3 Dynamic Object Binding and Perceptual Feedback Dynamic object binding first identifies which scene instance a rule addresses and then determines where that instance can be controlled in the current view. Semantic, appearance, and spatial consistency associate candidate instances with rule entities, and ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} stores these correspondences. Objects of the same category retain distinct identities, while viewpoint changes, occlusion, and reappearance preserve established bindings. For localized objects, camera projection and instance segmentation Ravi et al. (2024) provide spatiotemporal masks M i M_{i} , restricted by visibility and occlusion. Rules can update an object’s persistent state while it is invisible. Given an established 3D binding, the stored state is assigned to the projected region before generating the window in which the object first appears. A gate opened outside the view is therefore conditioned as open from its first appearance, without repeating the opening action. Effects on entirely unlocalized entities remain pending until reliable correspondences become available. First-appearance control thus depends on spatial grounding established before generation. The executed scene geometry guides layout, camera motion, and object motion, while effective states and changes form global and object-level visual descriptions. Each local condition specifies an identity, spatiotemporal support, and structured attribute targets. Surface changes use object surface support, while motion and deformation cover the current geometry and rule-executed trajectory, excluding foreground occluders and unrelated instances. Unknown attributes are omitted from local control, and completed changes persist as resulting-state conditions. Perception independently estimates identity, visibility, visual attributes, and action completion from generated frames, without receiving desired rule outcomes as answer cues. Evidence passing identity, confidence, and temporal validity checks updates bindings, local geometry, and ordinary observable state, and supplies events for subsequent rules that require visual confirmation. Rule-prescribed states and observed outcomes are recorded separately. If a gate appears closed despite an open-state requirement, the prescribed state is retained, and the observed discrepancy guides correction in subsequent generation windows. Feedback affects only windows generated after its acceptance, without rewriting delivered video or treating unconfirmed outcomes as successful. 3.4 Object Attribute State Replacement Object binding determines the support of an edit, and attribute state replacement adjusts its visual representation to the rule target. Choosing What to Observe: Budget-Paired Counterfactual Audits for Credible Evaluation of Visual Agents Ruiqi Liu Affiliation: Fudan University Institute of Medical Philosophy & Future AI (IMPF-AI) Jinming Li Mo Wang Affiliation: The University of Warwick Southern University of Science and Technology * Corresponding authors Yang Lu Yanlan Kang Affiliation: Fudan University Institute of Medical Philosophy & Future AI (IMPF-AI) Abstract Visual agents that read dense documents must ration a finite observation budget across candidate regions, yet answer accuracy conflates where an agent looks, how it adapts to the reads that remain, and how it answers once observation stops. We introduce budget-paired counterfactual audits , an evaluation protocol that holds public evidence and region bindings fixed while perturbing only the remaining budget or declared task parameters, and credits every acquired history with exact continuation values. The resulting accounting decomposes lost expected accuracy into stepwise acquisition loss and terminal decision loss, separating planning from fixed-role heuristics. Across forty paired routing anchors, five open-weight VLMs make 0/40 optimal branch-to-selector switches and incur 12.50–15.62 percentage points (pp) of anchor loss, a cost that low non-anchor averages (0.59–0.85 pp) conceal. In three-read hierarchies, first reads are nearly optimal (0.18–0.96 pp loss), whereas the second and third reads lose 22.20–26.76 pp. On thirty FUNSD forms, Qwen3-VL-8B’s one-crop selection gain over a shared uniform reader falls from 24.44 pp under curated references to an inconclusive 10.56 pp under the original references, and its two-crop pipeline trails native whole-image reading (70.0% versus 83.3%) while using twice the input tokens. Credible evaluation of visual agents therefore requires auditing complete observation histories against matched whole-image baselines, with transparent reference scoring. Figure 1 : Budget-paired counterfactual audit. (a) A form whose route field says which price table (A or B) holds the answer; numbered circles give the order of reads. With two reads left, a horizon-aware planner and a policy that always reads the route first make identical choices, so a single-budget test cannot separate them. With one read left, the route is worth less than either table (expected accuracy 0.50 versus 0.75), and only the planner switches. All five open-weight VLMs keep reading the route: 0/40 optimal switches. (b) Expected accuracy lost at each step of 160 three-read episodes per model: first reads are near-optimal (0.18–0.96 pp), while the second and third reads lose 22.20–26.76 pp. 1 Introduction Visual agents often work on dense documents from a low-resolution overview that exposes the layout but blurs fine text. Selective high-resolution crops recover local detail without processing every pixel [ 14 , 11 , 6 ] , which turns observation into a sequential decision problem whenever reads are limited. Consider an invoice whose routing field indicates which of two price tables applies. With two crops remaining, reading the routing field first directs the second crop to the active table. With one crop left, the same action exhausts the budget without revealing a price, and opening a table directly is strictly better. An observation is worth what it enables before the reads run out, not what it reveals in isolation. Answer accuracy on isolated test cases cannot see this distinction. Our key idea is to audit budget-paired counterfactuals : decisions whose public evidence and region bindings stay identical while only the remaining budget or the action-value boundary changes (Fig. 1 a). Such pairs separate policies that look identical under a single budget. A fixed-selector heuristic and a horizon-aware planner both open the routing field at b = 2 b=2 ; only the planner opens a branch at b = 1 b=1 . Detecting a behavioral gap is half of the problem; an evaluator must also price it across the whole rollout. Under an explicit task model, we compute exact finite-horizon continuation values and apply a performance-difference identity that attributes lost expected accuracy to each observation and to the final answer (Fig. 1 b). Applying the audit to five open-weight VLMs and two hosted models reveals a sharp divide between plausible first actions and effective sequential policies. None of the five open models makes a single optimal budget switch in forty pairs each, while GPT-5 mini switches in 48/48 pairs, so the behavior is attainable. In three-read hierarchies, three checkpoints make near-optimal first reads yet lose 22.20–26.76 pp on the routing steps that follow. On natural scanned forms, apparent selection gains move with the reference definition, and two-crop systems stay below native whole-image accuracy while consuming more calls and input tokens. In summary, we make three contributions: • Budget- and value-paired counterfactual tests that separate horizon-sensitive planning from fixed-role heuristics under identical public evidence. • Exact trajectory return accounting that decomposes end-to-end accuracy loss into stepwise acquisition loss and terminal decision loss. • An empirical audit across controlled decisions, complete rollouts and natural forms , showing that later-read routing dominates policy loss and that natural-document gains depend on reference definitions and whole-image comparators. 2 Related Work Selective visual observation. High-resolution benchmarks and visual search systems study how agents acquire detail beyond an overview [ 14 , 11 ] . FOVEA casts high-resolution vision as sequential Bayesian experimental design, using a coverage–resolution objective to refine crop proposals [ 6 ] . Interactive systems such as ReAct, VisualWebArena and SpatialEval further motivate evaluating decisions made across a sequence of observations [ 15 , 5 , 9 ] . We examine whether such choices respond to remaining budget and task value, with exact references for controlled cases. Auditing and crediting visual tools. The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use tests reliance on visual returns through policy comparisons, trajectory corruptions and interventions at fixed prefixes [ 13 ] . OPO compares alternative observations after shared prefixes to assign local evidence credit during training [ 10 ] . Our evaluator complements these interventions by assigning each legal alternative a cost in expected terminal accuracy under a declared model. Paired budgets and shifted value boundaries then test behavioral explanations, and return accounting locates the cost across a complete history (Table 1 ). AFABench’s CUBE-NM includes a context feature that identifies an informative block while providing no immediate label information [ 8 ] . We use the same routing principle to construct decisions whose optimal actions differ across matched budgets. 3 Method The framework combines a declared task model, paired interventions and an evaluator for complete observation histories. Applying the audit to five open-weight VLMs and two hosted models reveals a sharp divide between plausible first actions and effective sequential policies. None of the five open models makes a single optimal budget switch in forty pairs each, while GPT-5 mini switches in 48/48 pairs, so the behavior is attainable. In three-read hierarchies, three checkpoints make near-optimal first reads yet lose 22.20–26.76 pp on the routing steps that follow. On natural scanned forms, apparent selection gains move with the reference definition, and two-crop systems stay below native whole-image accuracy while consuming more calls and input tokens. High-resolution benchmarks and visual search systems study how agents acquire detail beyond an overview [ 14 , 11 ] . FOVEA casts high-resolution vision as sequential Bayesian experimental design, using a coverage–resolution objective to refine crop proposals [ 6 ] . Interactive systems such as ReAct, VisualWebArena and SpatialEval further motivate evaluating decisions made across a sequence of observations [ 15 , 5 , 9 ] . We examine whether such choices respond to remaining budget and task value, with exact references for controlled cases. Auditing and crediting visual tools. The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use tests reliance on visual returns through policy comparisons, trajectory corruptions and interventions at fixed prefixes [ 13 ] . OPO compares alternative observations after shared prefixes to assign local evidence credit during training [ 10 ] . Our evaluator complements these interventions by assigning each legal alternative a cost in expected terminal accuracy under a declared model. Paired budgets and shifted value boundaries then test behavioral explanations, and return accounting locates the cost across a complete history (Table 1 ). items.content: The Commission has now approved more than 20 State aid decisions on first-of-a-kind semiconductor facilities, bringing total public and private investment to over €33 billion. © monsitj The European Chips Act aims to boost Europe’s sovereignty and competitiveness in semiconductor technologies through three pillars of action. Today, the Commission reached a major milestone under the second pillar of the European Chips Act, which focuses on security and supply and resilience: the approval of more than 20 state aid decisions to support first-of-a-kind facilities in semiconductors. Together, these decisions have unlocked more than €33 billion in public and private investment. From wafers and chips to advanced packaging, testing and assembly, and from high specialised materials to power electronics, each project helps to strengthen and diversify Europe’s position across the semiconductor value chain and reduce strategic dependencies. Furthermore, these decisions, which concern investments across the EU, help to boost wider economic activity as well as advancing the EU’s technological sovereignty goals. Background The European Chips Act aims to reinforce the semiconductor ecosystem in the EU. It outlines three pillars of action to achieve this: Chips for Europe initiative Security of supply and resilience Monitoring and crisis response Pillar II, security of supply and resilience, focuses on supporting companies to manufacture chips in Europe, attracting investments and enhancing production capacities so Europe can compete on the global stage. These investments cover first-of-a-kind facilities – those that can bring additional capacity and innovation to the European semiconductor ecosystem. Last update 18 November 2026 Print as PDF

Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 18, 2026 Back to Top

Press Conference Materials Opening Statement Transcript (PDF) FOMC Transcripts and other historical materials 2020 FOMC Historical Documents FAQs Related Content Guide to the Summary of Economic Projections The term "monetary policy" refers to the actions undertaken by a central bank, such as the Federal Reserve, to influence the availability and cost of money and credit to help promote national economic goals. The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 gave the Federal Reserve responsibility for setting monetary policy. The Federal Reserve controls the three tools of monetary policy-- open market operations , the discount rate , and reserve requirements . The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is responsible for the discount rate and reserve requirements, and the Federal Open Market Committee is responsible for open market operations. Using the three tools, the Federal Reserve influences the demand for, and supply of, balances that depository institutions hold at Federal Reserve Banks and in this way alters the federal funds rate. The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which depository institutions lend balances at the Federal Reserve to other depository institutions overnight. Changes in the federal funds rate trigger a chain of events that affect other short-term interest rates, foreign exchange rates, long-term interest rates, the amount of money and credit, and, ultimately, a range of economic variables, including employment, output, and prices of goods and services. Structure of the FOMC The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) consists of twelve members--the seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; and four of the remaining eleven Reserve Bank presidents, who serve one-year terms on a rotating basis. The rotating seats are filled from the following four groups of Banks, one Bank president from each group: Boston, Philadelphia, and Richmond; Cleveland and Chicago; Atlanta, St. Louis, and Dallas; and Minneapolis, Kansas City, and San Francisco. Nonvoting Reserve Bank presidents attend the meetings of the Committee, participate in the discussions, and contribute to the Committee's assessment of the economy and policy options. The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings per year. At these meetings, the Committee reviews economic and financial conditions, determines the appropriate stance of monetary policy, and assesses the risks to its long-run goals of price stability and sustainable economic growth. For more information about the FOMC and monetary policy, see the " Monetary Policy " section of The Fed Explained: What the Central Bank Does .
